hook: Most of a big company's bytes are read hard for a short time, then almost never. So why not delete them?
title: Most bytes are old, cold, and still can't be deleted
body:
Most bytes at a big company are not profiles or messages. They are old photos, old logs and huge analytics tables. The pattern is always the same: written once, read heavily for a short time, then almost never read again.

You still cannot delete them. Some trains models, some is needed for audits, and some is a user's wedding photo from 2012. The job is to keep this cooling mass cheaply without losing any of it.
takeaway: Storage economics is about the cold majority, not the average byte.
deeper:
**Three tools, one problem:** The data lake is the storage under analytics, built for scanning huge tables. Tiering moves data to cheaper media as it cools. Archival keeps data for decades at the lowest cost, where retrieval in hours is fine.

**The fourth lever:** Retention decides how long data lives at all. It is often the strongest tool, because a deleted byte costs nothing.

**The mental shift:** Stop thinking about the average byte. Most bytes are cold, they get cold quickly, and each temperature deserves different media, different redundancy and even different datacenter designs.

**The running example:** A global app with 1 billion users. Its lake holds event logs, daily database snapshots and derived tables, and its photos are kept until the user deletes them. Each of these cools at its own speed, so each needs its own rules.

quiz.q: A teammate proposes deleting every object nobody has read in 90 days to cut the storage bill. What kinds of value would that destroy?
quiz.a: Data that trains ML models, data required for audits, and irreplaceable user content like a 2012 wedding photo. Cold data is rarely read, not worthless.

mcq.q: What access pattern do most bytes at a big company follow?
options: Written once, read heavily briefly, then almost never
Read at the same steady rate for many years
Rewritten daily as users update their profiles
Read rarely at first, then more often as they age
mcq.why: Photos, logs and analytics tables get most of their reads soon after they are written, then go cold but must still be kept.

section: 7.1 What a data lake really is
hook: Spark, Trino, Hive and Flink all query the same table. Nobody made a copy. How?
title: One copy of the data, many engines reading it
body:
If every analytics tool kept its own copy of the data, you would pay for many copies and watch them drift apart. A **data lake** avoids that. It is a large, shared store of raw and processed files, and Spark, Presto/Trino, Hive and Flink all read and write the same files.

The files usually use open **columnar** formats like Parquet or ORC. Each column is stored together, so a query reads only the columns it needs.
takeaway: Open formats turn one copy of data into a shared platform.
deeper:
**Why columnar pays:** A table has 200 columns and a query needs 3. A row-oriented file forces the engine to read all 200. A columnar file fetches only the 3 column chunks. Values of one type sit together, so run-length and dictionary encodings compress them well.

**Why open matters:** A Spark batch job can write a table that Trino queries minutes later, with no export step. One copy serves many teams and tools.

**The catch:** Openness pushes chores onto the platform team. Someone must manage the files themselves: how big they are, which ones belong to a table, and when old ones get deleted. Small files, compaction and tiering all follow from that freedom.

**The one-line version:** A lake is not a product. It is a pile of open files plus the discipline to keep them tidy.

quiz.q: A query needs 3 columns of a 200-column table. Why does a columnar file make it far cheaper than a row-oriented one?
quiz.a: Each column is stored together, so the engine fetches only the 3 needed column chunks instead of every full row. Similar values sitting together also compress better, so fewer bytes are read.

mcq.q: Why can Spark and Trino query the same lake table without copying it?
options: Both read the same files in open formats like Parquet
The lake converts each file for each engine on read
Each engine keeps its own private cached copy
The storage layer runs the queries for both engines
mcq.why: Lake files sit in shared storage in open columnar formats that every engine understands, so one copy serves them all.

section: 7.1 What a data lake really is
hook: You need a giant cluster for one afternoon's job. Why don't you have to copy any data onto it?
title: Storage stays put; compute clusters come and go
body:
A big analytics job may need a huge cluster for a few hours. If the data lived on the compute machines, you would copy petabytes in and out each time.

Lakes avoid this with **separation of storage and compute**. The files sit in one big storage system. Compute clusters come and go. You can add another query engine without copying the data. Storage grows with what you keep, compute grows with the work you run, and each is sized and paid for separately.
takeaway: Size storage for what you keep and compute for what you run.
deeper:
**The coupled alternative:** When every storage server is also a compute server, disk and CPU come in a fixed ratio. A team needing more disk but not more CPU still buys both. First-generation HDFS lakes worked this way.

**The price:** Every read now crosses the network, since the data is not on the machine doing the work. That became acceptable because datacenter networks grew fast and flat, and because columnar formats cut how many bytes each query pulls.

**The bonus:** Many engines share one copy. A new engine needs no private dataset, so nothing drifts and nothing is paid for twice.

**The arc:** Much of the move from HDFS to object stores was about breaking the tie between disks and CPUs.

quiz.q: Your lake's data doubles every year, but query load stays flat. Compare the hardware bill on a coupled HDFS cluster and on a separated design.
quiz.a: Coupled: every new disk arrives inside a server with CPU you don't need, so you pay for idle compute. Separated: you add only storage and keep compute clusters the same size.

mcq.q: What does separating storage from compute cost a lake?
options: Every read goes over the network
Data must be copied for each new engine
Compute clusters must run permanently
Files can no longer use columnar formats
mcq.why: The data no longer sits on the machine doing the work, so reads cross the network; fast networks and columnar formats make that acceptable.

section: 7.1 What a data lake really is
hook: Nobody cares if fetching one event from a data lake takes 5 ms. So what does the lake optimize for?
title: Lakes are built for bytes per second, not milliseconds
body:
A serving database lives or dies on milliseconds, because a user waits on every request. A lake has no such user. Nobody needs a single event in 5 ms. Analysts need to scan billions of rows per second.

So the lake optimizes for **throughput** (bytes per second) and cost per byte, not latency. In a global app with 1 billion users, it holds append-only event logs growing many petabytes a year, daily database snapshots, and derived tables.
takeaway: When nobody waits on one record, optimize for the scan and the bill.
deeper:
**What it frees up:** Dense hard drives, aggressive erasure coding, network reads instead of local reads, and large files that stream efficiently. None of these would survive a latency budget of a few milliseconds.

**Why small files hurt:** A system tuned to stream big sequential reads suffers when forced into millions of tiny requests. That mismatch drives a whole class of lake problems.

**Three data types, three ages:** Event logs record every click, view and message-send; they grow forever and cool quickly. Snapshots of the profile and message databases are copied in each day for analysis. Derived tables, such as daily active users, ad reports and ML training sets, may be read again and again.

**The payoff:** Because each type ages differently, each later gets its own tiering and retention rule.

quiz.q: An architect proposes putting the whole lake on low-latency flash to speed up analysts' daily scans. What's wrong with the reasoning?
quiz.a: Scans are limited by throughput and cost per byte, not per-request latency. Flash buys milliseconds nobody waits on, at a much higher price per byte than dense disks.

mcq.q: Which pair of metrics does a data lake's storage optimize?
options: Throughput and cost per byte
Latency and IOPS per request
Write latency and consistency
Cache hit rate and p99 latency
mcq.why: Analysts scan billions of rows per second and nobody waits on a single event, so bytes per second and cost per byte dominate.

hook: Your lake is slow. Is it the engine, the table format, the file format, the storage, or the disks?
title: A lake is a stack: engines, tables, files, storage, media
body:
When a lake misbehaves, the first question is which layer owns the problem. Top to bottom: compute engines (Spark, Trino, Flink, BigQuery); table format and catalog (Hive, Iceberg, Hudi, Delta); file format (Parquet, ORC, Capacitor); storage layer (HDFS, S3, GCS, Tectonic, Colossus); and media (HDD, flash, tape).

The core three have separate jobs. **Storage** keeps bytes and names. The **file format** lays out rows and columns inside a file. The **table format** tracks which files make up a table at each point in time.
takeaway: Name the layer before you name the fix.
deeper:
**Three or five:** The core lake has three layers: storage, file format and table format. Engines sit above them and physical media below, which makes five in the full picture.

**What each one knows:** Storage knows paths or object keys, never what a table is. The file format decides layout inside one file, such as grouping values by column. The table format gives transactions and snapshots, because it records which files belong to each version.

**Why it pays off:** Uber swapped its storage from HDFS to Google Cloud Storage and left the layers above untouched. Netflix built a new table format, Iceberg, because the storage below it could not rename atomically. Colossus tiers at the media level, invisible to everything above.

**Diagnosis in practice:** Slow commits on S3 are a table-format problem. Small files are a storage and table-maintenance problem.

quiz.q: Hive jobs on S3 sometimes expose half-written output to readers. Which layer should you change, and why won't switching object-store vendors help?
quiz.a: The table format. Object stores cannot rename a directory atomically, so commits must move into metadata, as Iceberg does. Another object store has the same gap.

mcq.q: Which lake layer knows which files make up a table at a given moment?
options: The table format, such as Iceberg
The storage layer, such as S3
The file format, such as Parquet
The compute engine, such as Spark
mcq.why: Storage only knows bytes and names, and the file format only lays out one file; the table format tracks table membership over time.

hook: From 2008 to 2020, most big lakes trusted every file name to one machine's memory. Why did that work?
title: HDFS: one NameNode in RAM, blocks copied 3× on DataNodes
body:
From about 2008 to 2020, most big lakes ran on HDFS, the Hadoop Distributed File System. One **NameNode** holds the whole directory tree in memory. Blocks live on many **DataNodes**, and by default each block is copied 3 times.

It worked because of **data locality**: the scheduler runs a task on the machine that holds its block, so the read skips the network. Add open-source software on cheap commodity disks, and HDFS was the obvious choice.
takeaway: HDFS moved the computation to the data, and paid for it later.
deeper:
**Why locality mattered:** Datacenter networks had not yet become fast and flat, so reading a block locally instead of across racks was a real win. HDFS built its whole shape around that.

**Three bills came due:** The NameNode keeps every file and block in RAM, so one machine's memory caps the namespace. 3× replication means every PB of data needs 3 PB of disk. And because DataNodes double as compute nodes, storage and compute grow together whether you need both or not.

**What came next:** Each bill pushed companies toward object-store lakes, or toward custom systems like Meta's Tectonic.

**Why learn it now:** The HDFS design is the baseline. Almost every feature of a modern lake is an answer to one of those three bills.

quiz.q: A job reads 1 TB on an HDFS cluster where every task runs on the node holding its block. Ideally, how much crosses the network, and why did that matter then?
quiz.a: Almost none: data locality means each task reads its block from local disk. That mattered before datacenter networks became fast and flat.

mcq.q: Where does HDFS keep its file metadata?
options: In one NameNode's memory
Spread across all DataNodes' disks
In a replicated SQL database
Inside each block's header
mcq.why: A single NameNode holds the whole directory tree in RAM; DataNodes store only the blocks.

hook: An HDFS cluster can have petabytes of free disk and still fall over. What actually runs out?
title: HDFS runs out of files before it runs out of bytes
body:
An HDFS cluster can have plenty of free disk and still be in trouble. Every file and every block is tracked in the **NameNode**'s RAM, on one server.

More files means more memory. More memory means longer garbage-collection pauses and more lock contention. Because a single machine holds the whole namespace, that machine caps how many files the cluster can hold. Petabytes in large files are fine. Millions of tiny files are not.
takeaway: The NameNode counts files, not bytes. Tiny files spend its memory fastest.
deeper:
**A public example:** Uber wrote in 2018 that its HDFS data grew more than 400% in 2017. In late 2016, NameNode queue time passed 500 ms, against a normal level of under 10 ms. Every metadata operation in the cluster slowed down.

**The toolbox:** Uber used ViewFs, which puts several physical namespaces behind one virtual view, splitting metadata across NameNodes while users see one tree. It also upgraded, tuned garbage collection and built small-file merge tools. Merging is the most direct lever, since every file removed frees NameNode memory.

**The real lesson:** The NameNode problem is a file-count problem, not a byte-count problem. That is why the small-files problem is welded to HDFS, and why object stores, with no single metadata server, looked so attractive.

quiz.q: Two HDFS clusters store 1 PB each. One uses 1 GB files, the other 1 MB files. Which gets NameNode trouble, and what symptoms appear first?
quiz.a: The 1 MB cluster, with about 1,000 times more files, each held in NameNode RAM. Expect longer garbage-collection pauses, lock contention and slow metadata operations.

mcq.q: What limits how many files an HDFS cluster can hold?
options: The NameNode's RAM
Total DataNode disk space
Network bandwidth between racks
The replication factor of 3
mcq.why: Every file and block lives in the single NameNode's memory, so its RAM caps the namespace.

hook: Every petabyte on classic HDFS costs 3 petabytes of disk. HDFS 3 cut that. What did it give up?
title: RS(6,3) cuts HDFS overhead from 200% to about 50%
body:
Classic HDFS stores every block 3 times, so each PB of data needs 3 PB of disk: 200% overhead. HDFS 3 added **erasure coding**, with RS(6,3) as the default policy. Data is split into 6 chunks, plus 3 parity chunks computed from them. Overhead drops to about 50%.

The price: erasure-coded files lose some features, such as append, and most reads go across racks.
takeaway: Erasure coding trades features and locality for disk. Cold, stable data takes that deal.
deeper:
**How RS(6,3) works:** 9 chunks hold 6 chunks' worth of data. Any 6 of the 9 can rebuild the original, so it survives losing 3 chunks while using 1.5× raw capacity instead of 3×. At lake scale, 1.5 PB instead of 3 PB per PB stored is a huge saving.

**Why replicas survived:** No append clashes with files that grow over time. Chunks are spread out, so reads cross racks and data locality weakens. Rebuilding a lost chunk means reading several others.

**The pattern:** Meta's Tectonic encodes long-lived warehouse data with RS(9,6) and short-lived shuffle output with RS(3,3). Meta also moved warm photos from 3.6× to 2.1× effective replication. The colder and more stable the data, the more aggressive the code it can take.

quiz.q: A team wants RS(6,3) on a directory where a service appends to log files all day. What goes wrong, and what would you suggest?
quiz.a: Erasure-coded HDFS files can't be appended to, so the writer breaks. Keep actively growing files replicated 3×, and use RS(6,3) for stable data.

mcq.q: What does HDFS give up when a file moves from 3× replication to RS(6,3)?
options: Append support, and most reads go cross-rack
Durability against a single disk failure
The ability to store Parquet files
Compatibility with the NameNode
mcq.why: Erasure-coded files lose features like append, and chunks are spread out so reads cross racks, in exchange for about 50% overhead.

predict.q: HDFS 3's default erasure code, RS(6,3), replaces 3× replication. What storage overhead does it have?
options: About 50%
About 100%
About 150%

hook: Your HDFS lake needs more disk and no more CPU. Why are you buying CPUs anyway?
title: On HDFS, buying disk means buying CPU too
body:
On HDFS, storage and compute are welded together. A DataNode is also a compute node, because **data locality** only works if the machine storing a block can run the task that reads it.

So the cluster's shape is fixed: disk and CPU come in the ratio of the server you buy. Lake data grows relentlessly, while compute demand rises and falls. A coupled cluster must be sized for whichever is bigger, leaving the other idle.
takeaway: A coupled cluster is sized for its bottleneck and wastes the rest.
deeper:
**A deliberate choice:** The coupling was not an accident. It was the price of HDFS's best feature, running tasks where the data lives.

**Why the two grow apart:** Event logs are append-only and retention is long, so storage keeps climbing. Compute follows analysts and job schedules, which fluctuate. Over the years, the ratio you bought drifts away from the ratio you need.

**The fix:** Separate the two. Storage becomes dense, disk-heavy machines or a rented object store. Compute runs on clusters sized to today's workload and shut down when idle.

**The bigger picture:** This was one of three reasons companies moved lakes from HDFS to object storage around 2015 to 2020, alongside the NameNode memory limit and the cost of 3× replication.

quiz.q: Why couldn't HDFS simply put storage and compute on separate machines while keeping its main advantage?
quiz.a: Its advantage was data locality: running tasks on the node holding the block. Separate machines would send every read over the network, exactly what locality avoided.

mcq.q: Why did HDFS DataNodes also serve as compute nodes?
options: Data locality needed tasks to run where blocks live
The NameNode could not track separate compute nodes
Replication needed CPU on every storage node
Commodity servers could not be bought without CPUs
mcq.why: Locality means running a task on the machine holding its block, which only works if storage machines also compute.

hook: Uber's HDFS data grew more than 400% in one year. Where did the strain show up?
title: Uber's NameNode queue went from under 10 ms to 500 ms
body:
Uber wrote in 2018 that its HDFS data grew more than 400% in 2017. The NameNode, which holds every file and block in one server's RAM, could not keep up. In late 2016, its queue time passed 500 ms. Normal is under 10 ms.

That queue ran more than 50 times normal, and every metadata operation waited in it: directory listing, every file open, every job writing output.
takeaway: When one server holds all metadata, growth shows up as queueing everywhere.
deeper:
**ViewFs splits namespaces:** Several physical namespaces sit behind one virtual view. Each NameNode holds part of the tree, while users and jobs still see a single one. It attacks the one-namespace limit directly.

**Tuning and upgrades:** Garbage-collection tuning shortens the pauses that a huge in-memory heap causes. Upgrades brought in fixes from newer releases.

**Small-file merging:** Fewer files means less for the NameNode to track at all. The cluster can hold petabytes fine; what hurts is the number of objects. That makes merging the most direct lever of the four.

**What came next:** Uber had already built Hudi on HDFS, described in March 2017, to handle mutable trip data. In 2024 it announced a move of batch analytics and ML training from on-premises Hadoop to Google Cloud. A metadata server is a single queue in front of every job.

quiz.q: Uber's HDFS disks had room to spare, yet jobs crawled in late 2016. Why would merging small files help?
quiz.a: The NameNode keeps every file and block in RAM. Fewer, larger files mean less memory, shorter garbage-collection pauses and less lock contention, so its queue shrinks.

mcq.q: What did Uber's ViewFs change do for its overloaded HDFS?
options: Put several namespaces behind one virtual view
Moved all its files into Google Cloud Storage
Replaced 3× replication with erasure coding
Cached file blocks in NameNode memory
mcq.why: ViewFs splits metadata across several physical namespaces while users still see one tree, relieving any single NameNode.

hook: Lakes love big files. Streaming jobs produce millions of tiny ones. Why can't they just write big files?
title: Lakes want 128 MB-1 GB files and get millions of tiny ones
body:
The small-files problem is the most common pain in any lake. Lakes work best with files of 128 MB to 1 GB. But streaming jobs flush a file every few minutes per partition, for freshness. And every parallel task writes its own output.

The result is millions of files of a few KB or MB. Total bytes are fine. The sheer file count is what swamps metadata, request budgets and query planners.
takeaway: Small files are the tax on freshness, and you pay it forever.
deeper:
**Not a bug:** Small files are a side effect of how data arrives. Freshness pushes jobs to flush often. Parallelism makes each task write separately. Hundreds of partitions times frequent flushes multiplies file counts fast.

**Permanent, so manage it:** You cannot design the problem away, only manage it continuously. That is why compaction runs as an ongoing platform service, not a one-time cleanup.

**It follows you across generations:** On HDFS the cost lands on NameNode memory. On object stores, with no single metadata server, it shifts to per-request latency and fees, because every file needs its own LIST entry and GET. Both suffer at the file-format level too, since tiny Parquet files have tiny column chunks.

**The punchline:** Moving from HDFS to S3 changes who pays for small files. It does not make them free.

quiz.q: A team moves its lake from HDFS to S3, expecting the small-files problem to vanish since S3 has no NameNode. What do they find?
quiz.a: The cost moves instead of vanishing. Each file still needs its own LIST entry and GET, with latency and a fee, and tiny files still compress and plan badly.

mcq.q: Why do streaming jobs create so many small lake files?
options: They flush often per partition, and each task writes its own file
Object stores split large uploads into small pieces
Parquet cannot hold files larger than a few MB
Compaction breaks big files apart for parallelism
mcq.why: Frequent flushes for freshness, multiplied by partitions and parallel tasks, produce millions of files of a few KB or MB.

hook: Store 1 GB as one file or as 10,000 small ones. Same bytes. Why is one version so much slower?
title: 1 GB as 10,000 files costs 10,000 requests
body: Small files hurt in three ways. **Metadata**: on HDFS each file costs NameNode memory; on object stores each needs its own LIST entry and GET. **Requests**: 1 GB as 10,000 files of 100 KB takes 10,000 requests, each with fixed latency, often tens of ms, and on S3 a price. **Compression and planning**: tiny files have tiny column chunks, so Parquet compresses worse, and the planner must open every file's footer.
takeaway: Every per-file cost scales with file count. Fix the count, fix all three.
deeper:
**Requests you can feel:** One 1 GB file is one long sequential stream. 10,000 files of 100 KB are 10,000 round trips, each paying setup latency before a byte moves. Parallelism helps, but the overhead dominates, and on S3 every GET is billed.

**Compression, the subtle one:** Columnar formats win by finding long runs of similar values inside a column chunk. A file with a few thousand rows makes short chunks, so run-length and dictionary encoding have little to work with.

**Planning, the sneaky one:** Before a query runs, the engine reads each Parquet footer for schema and column statistics. With millions of files, planning becomes a big job of its own.

**The good news:** All three costs scale with file count. Compaction lowers the count, so it fixes all three at once.

quiz.q: A dashboard query over one day of data is slow, though the day is only 1 GB. It's stored as 10,000 files. Give two separate reasons it's slow.
quiz.a: Each of 10,000 requests pays fixed latency, often tens of ms. And the planner must open every file's footer, while tiny column chunks compress poorly.

mcq.q: Why do tiny Parquet files compress worse than large ones?
options: Short column chunks give encodings fewer repeats
Parquet disables compression below a size limit
Object stores recompress small files poorly
Small files must be stored row by row
mcq.why: Run-length and dictionary encoding thrive on long runs of similar values; a tiny file's column chunks are too short to exploit them.

predict.q: You read 1 GB stored as 100 KB files. How many requests does that take?

hook: One table, 1 TB a day, a flush every 5 minutes. Innocent settings. How many files after a year?
title: One streaming table, 52 million files a year
body:
Take a table receiving 1 TB a day from a streaming job with 500 partitions that flushes every 5 minutes. That is 500 × 288 = 144,000 files a day, averaging about 7 MB. After a year: about 52 million files.

Store the same data as 512 MB files and you get about 2,000 files a day, or 730,000 a year. That is 70 times fewer objects to list, open and track.

stat.label: files a year from one streaming table

takeaway: File count is partitions times flushes. Both knobs look harmless alone.
deeper:
**Where 288 comes from:** A day has 1,440 minutes. Flushing every 5 minutes gives 288 flushes. Multiply by 500 partitions and you get 144,000 files daily. 1 TB divided by 144,000 is about 7 MB per file, far below the 128 MB to 1 GB sweet spot.

**What 52 million means:** On HDFS, every one of those files sits in NameNode memory. On an object store, query planning may list and open a large share of them.

**Nothing about the data changed:** The 512 MB version holds exactly the same bytes. Only the layout differs.

**The levers:** Keep small, frequent files for freshness while a partition is open, then compact it into large files once it closes. Or cut partitions or flush frequency, at the cost of freshness.

quiz.q: Same 1 TB/day table, but the team cuts to 250 partitions and flushes every 10 minutes. Roughly how many files a day now, and what did they give up?
quiz.a: 250 × 144 = 36,000 files a day, a quarter of before, averaging about 28 MB. They gave up freshness, since each partition now flushes only every 10 minutes.

mcq.q: In the 1 TB/day example, why is the average file only about 7 MB?
options: 500 partitions × 288 flushes split 1 TB into 144,000 files
Parquet caps each file at 7 MB by default
The object store splits uploads into 7 MB parts
Compaction rewrites files down to 7 MB each
mcq.why: 500 partitions flushing 288 times a day make 144,000 files; 1 TB spread across them is about 7 MB each.

predict.q: A table gets 1 TB a day from 500 partitions, each flushing every 5 minutes. How many files after one year?
options: About 52 million
About 5 million
About 500,000

hook: You rewrite a live table's files while queries are running on it. How does no reader ever see a mix?
title: Compaction: rewrite small files big, then swap atomically
body:
Small files pile up forever unless something merges them. **Compaction** is a background job that reads many small files and rewrites them as fewer large ones. Then it updates the table metadata so readers switch to the new files atomically: a query sees all old files or all new ones, never a mix.

The old files are deleted later, so queries still reading them don't break.
takeaway: Compact once, after the writers have left.
deeper:
**Why the swap is safe:** Table formats such as Iceberg and Hudi record which files make up the table at each snapshot. Readers that started before the swap keep their snapshot. New readers get the compacted one.

**The costs:** The job reads and writes the data again. That is write amplification: compact the same data three times and you have written it four times. It competes with production jobs for cluster capacity. And it can conflict with writers on the same partition, forcing retries.

**The usual design:** Write small files quickly for freshness. Compact a partition once it is closed, for example once the hour has passed. No writer touches a closed partition, so conflicts disappear, and the data is rewritten once instead of again and again.

quiz.q: A team compacts each hourly partition every 10 minutes while it's still open, and sees retries and a high write bill. What should they change, and why?
quiz.a: Compact only after the hour closes. No writers remain, so there are no conflicts or retries, and each byte is rewritten once instead of repeatedly, cutting write amplification.

mcq.q: You compact the same data three times. How many times has it been written in total?
options: Four
Three
Six
Two
mcq.why: The original write plus three compaction rewrites makes four; that repeated rewriting is compaction's write amplification.

hook: Every team promises to compact its tables and expire old snapshots. At scale, some never do. What's the fix?
title: LinkedIn made table cleanup a platform, not a chore
body:
Leave table maintenance to each team and some forget, some do it wrong, and costs creep up unseen. LinkedIn built **OpenHouse**, a control plane for lakehouse tables, in production since late 2022. It stores Iceberg tables on HDFS and runs maintenance as scheduled Spark jobs: snapshot expiration, orphan file deletion, manifest compaction, retention, and cross-datacenter snapshot replication.

At scale, cleanup is not something each team should remember. It is a platform service.
takeaway: Hygiene nobody owns never happens. Make the platform own it.
deeper:
**What each job fixes:** Snapshot expiration removes old table versions, which would otherwise pin old files forever. Orphan file deletion removes files from failed jobs that no snapshot references. Manifest compaction shrinks the metadata files Iceberg uses to track data files, so planning stays fast. Retention purges data and expires partitions past their allowed age. Snapshot replication keeps copies in other datacenters.

**Why central wins:** Every table on the platform gets the same hygiene by default, whether or not its owners think about it.

**The retention link:** Deleted data lives on in derived tables and training sets. Building retention into the table platform itself helps make deletion policies real.

**Keep the fleet, add governance:** LinkedIn stays on its large owned HDFS fleet and adds central table governance on top.

quiz.q: Your lake's storage bill grows every month, though ingest is flat. Which OpenHouse-style jobs would you check first, and why?
quiz.a: Snapshot expiration, orphan file deletion and retention. Old snapshots pin files that should be gone, failed jobs leave unreferenced files, and expired data may never be purged.

mcq.q: What is the main lesson of LinkedIn's OpenHouse?
options: Table maintenance should run as a central platform service
Iceberg tables should move off HDFS to cloud storage
Compaction should be skipped to save cluster capacity
Each team should write its own cleanup scripts
mcq.why: OpenHouse schedules compaction, expiration, cleanup and retention for every table, so no team has to remember to do it.

hook: Between 2015 and 2020, lake after lake left HDFS for object storage. What exactly were they escaping?
title: Object stores fixed all three HDFS pains at once
body:
Around 2015 to 2020, many companies moved their lakes from HDFS to object storage: S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob or an internal equivalent. Each reason answers an HDFS pain. There is no single NameNode, so the file-count limit goes away. The provider runs erasure coding and replication, so there is no 3× copy to manage. Storage and compute scale independently, so compute clusters can be ephemeral.

One cost stayed: per-request charges.
takeaway: A migration that fixes three problems still hands you new ones to own.
deeper:
**The new cost model:** Instead of buying servers, you pay per GB-month plus per request. Request counts, and therefore file counts, become a line item on the bill. Small files stay painful; they just hurt in a new place.

**What the move cost:** Every read now crosses the network, so data locality is gone. Object stores also lack atomic directory renames, which old Hive-style tables relied on to commit jobs.

**What filled the gaps:** Table formats like Iceberg and Hudi track files in metadata instead of directory listings, so they became essential in the second generation.

**Different paths:** Netflix runs its warehouse on S3. Uber is moving to Google Cloud Storage. LinkedIn stayed on HDFS with Iceberg. Meta built its own exabyte-scale system, Tectonic.

quiz.q: After moving a lake from HDFS to S3, a team's metadata stalls vanish, but the monthly bill shows millions of GET charges. What happened?
quiz.a: The NameNode limit went away, but per-request cost remained. Every small file still needs its own LIST entry and GET, and S3 bills each one.

mcq.q: Which cost did moving a lake from HDFS to object storage NOT remove?
options: Per-file request cost
The NameNode memory limit
Managing 3× replicas yourself
Buying CPU along with disk
mcq.why: Object stores drop the NameNode, handle redundancy and decouple compute, but each file still costs LIST and GET requests.

hook: Object-store lakes send every single read over the network. Why isn't that a disaster?
title: Every read crosses the network, and scans stay fast
body:
HDFS's headline feature was **data locality**: run the task where the block lives. Object-store lakes throw that away. Compute never sits on the machine holding the data, so every read goes over the network.

It works for two reasons. Datacenter networks became fast and flat, so reaching any storage server is cheap. And columnar formats like Parquet read only the columns a query needs, so far fewer bytes cross the wire.
takeaway: Locality was a workaround for slow networks. Fast networks retired it.
deeper:
**Why the trade flipped:** Locality mattered when pulling data across racks was a bottleneck. As networks improved, flexibility became worth more than locality.

**Columnar multiplies it:** A query touching 5 of 100 columns pulls only those column chunks. The network carries a small slice of the table, while many storage servers together supply high bandwidth.

**The trade in one row:** HDFS lakes have locality; object-store lakes read everything over the network. In return, scaling compute separately goes from hard to easy.

**A quiet irony:** Erasure-coded HDFS had already given up much of its locality, since most reads of RS(6,3) data cross racks anyway. The industry did not abandon locality in one leap. It stopped paying for it once networks and file formats made it far less valuable.

quiz.q: An engineer argues that object-store lakes must be slower than HDFS because they lose data locality. Which facts undercut the argument?
quiz.a: Datacenter networks became fast and flat, so remote reads are cheap. Columnar formats read only the needed columns. And erasure-coded HDFS reads cross racks anyway.

mcq.q: What made giving up data locality acceptable for object-store lakes?
options: Fast, flat networks and columnar formats
Larger disks on every compute node
Caching every file in compute memory
Replicating data into every cluster
mcq.why: Remote reads became cheap on fast, flat networks, and columnar formats cut the bytes each query pulls.

hook: On HDFS, renaming a directory is instant and all-or-nothing. On S3 the same step can fail halfway. Why?
title: Object stores can't rename a directory atomically
body:
Old Hive-style tables committed a job by renaming a temporary directory into place. On HDFS that is one metadata operation on the NameNode: readers see nothing or everything.

Object stores have no real directories, only keys that share a prefix. Renaming a "directory" means copying and deleting every object, one by one. It is slow, and it can fail halfway, leaving readers with partial output. Table formats like **Iceberg** fix this by tracking files in metadata instead.
takeaway: On an object store, a directory is a naming habit, not a thing.
deeper:
**Why rename was a commit:** A job writes output to a temporary directory, then renames it to the final path. On a file system that single step makes the result appear all at once.

**What breaks on objects:** The rename takes time proportional to the number of files and can stop midway. Readers may see partial results. Listing a prefix to discover a table's files is itself slow when there are many.

**Iceberg's move:** Stop treating the directory as the source of truth. Table metadata lists the data files of each snapshot, and a commit atomically swaps a pointer to a new metadata version. Planning reads that list instead of walking prefixes.

**The summary row:** HDFS has atomic rename. Object-store lakes do not, and need a table format. That gap is one main reason Iceberg was created.

quiz.q: A Hive job on S3 crashes midway through its final rename. What might a reader see, and how would Iceberg have avoided it?
quiz.a: Some new output mixed with missing files, since objects were copied one by one. Iceberg commits by atomically swapping a metadata pointer, so readers see the old snapshot or the new one.

mcq.q: Why is renaming a directory on an object store unsafe as a commit?
options: It copies and deletes objects one by one
Object stores forbid renames entirely
Renames lock the whole bucket while running
Renamed objects lose their metadata
mcq.why: Directories are just key prefixes, so a rename is many separate copy-and-delete operations that can fail partway.

hook: HDFS and object-store lakes differ in six ways. Which difference quietly turns file counts into money?
title: HDFS vs object store: locality and rename vs elastic scale
body:
Side by side, the two generations trade opposite strengths. HDFS keeps metadata in one NameNode (or a federation) in RAM, offers data locality and atomic rename, and uses 3× replicas or RS(6,3). Object stores spread metadata across the provider, handle redundancy themselves and let compute scale separately, but offer no locality and no atomic rename.

The quiet difference is cost: HDFS means buying servers, while object stores charge per GB-month plus requests.
takeaway: On pay-per-request storage, every design flaw arrives as an invoice line.
deeper:
**Reading it as trades:** HDFS wins on locality and file-system semantics, but concentrates limits in the NameNode and couples storage to compute. Object stores win on elastic scale and operational simplicity, but need extra machinery, a table format, for safe commits.

**The cost row:** Buying servers is a capital expense sized in advance. Paying per GB-month plus requests is an operating expense that tracks usage. With per-request billing, file counts and access patterns land on the monthly bill, so small files and tiering become finance questions, not just performance ones.

**The middle ground:** Many companies ended up between the columns. LinkedIn stays on HDFS but adds Iceberg through OpenHouse. Uber is moving to Google Cloud Storage while keeping the HDFS API. Meta built Tectonic rather than choosing either.

quiz.q: Your CFO asks why compacting small files matters more after moving from HDFS to S3. What's the answer?
quiz.a: On HDFS, extra files cost NameNode memory on servers already bought. On S3, every file adds billed LIST and GET requests each month, so file count sits directly on the bill.

mcq.q: Which property does an HDFS lake have that an object-store lake lacks?
options: Atomic directory rename
Provider-managed redundancy
Easy independent compute scaling
Pay-per-request pricing
mcq.why: HDFS renames a directory in one NameNode operation; object stores need a table format to commit atomically.

section: 7.3.1 Netflix: the S3 lake and the birth of Iceberg
hook: Netflix's Hive tables on S3 hit two walls. The fix became an Apache project. What were the walls?
title: Netflix built Iceberg because Hive on S3 was slow and unsafe
body:
Netflix runs its data warehouse on Amazon S3, with compute clusters kept separate. Hive tables on S3 had two problems. They were slow to plan, because finding a table's files meant listing directories. And they were unsafe to change, because there was no atomic commit.

So Netflix engineers created **Iceberg**, later donated to Apache. It keeps an explicit, versioned list of each table's files in metadata, and commits by swapping to a new version atomically.
takeaway: On an object store, the table format must do the file system's old job.
deeper:
**Two problems, one root:** Both came from object-store semantics. Listing a prefix is slow when there are many objects, so planning dragged. There is no atomic rename, so a commit could leave readers seeing partial output.

**One fix for both:** Planning reads Iceberg's metadata instead of listing directories. Commits swap to a new metadata version in one step, so readers see the old table or the new one.

**Why S3 at all:** Netflix is the cloud-first company among the big lakes: S3 for storage, Iceberg and Parquet above it, and separate compute.

**The lasting principle:** When you move from a file system to an object store, jobs the file system did quietly, such as knowing which files belong to a table and changing them atomically, must move up a layer.

quiz.q: A team moves Hive tables from HDFS to S3 unchanged. Queries take ages to start, and a failed job left a half-visible partition. Which responsibility now needs a new owner?
quiz.a: Knowing which files belong to a table, and changing that atomically. On S3 it must move into a table format like Iceberg, which tracks files in versioned metadata.

mcq.q: Why did Netflix engineers create Iceberg?
options: Hive tables on S3 were slow to plan and unsafe to change
S3 could not store Parquet files efficiently
HDFS NameNodes ran out of memory at Netflix
Spark could not read tables stored on S3
mcq.why: Directory listings made planning slow and missing atomic commits made changes unsafe; Iceberg tracks files in metadata instead.

section: 7.3.2 Uber: from HDFS with Hudi to Google Cloud Storage
hook: A trip gets a rating days after it ends. On HDFS, where files can't change, how do you record it?
title: Uber's Hudi: updating immutable HDFS data within minutes
body:
HDFS files are immutable, but Uber's trip data keeps changing: a trip gets a rating, a fare is corrected. Rewriting whole partitions for each change was too slow.

So Uber built **Hudi** (Hadoop Upserts Deletes and Incrementals), described publicly in March 2017. Hudi keeps metadata about commit times and file versions. That lets it apply updates to HDFS data within minutes, and lets downstream jobs pull only the changes since a given time.
takeaway: Immutable files can hold mutable data if metadata says which version is current.
deeper:
**The mismatch:** Lake storage is built for write-once data, but business records like trips are mutable. Without Hudi, each change meant rewriting whole partitions, which was expensive and delayed freshness.

**How versions help:** Hudi writes new versions of only the affected files and records which version is current. That gives upserts (update or insert) and deletes on top of immutable storage.

**The incremental half:** Every change carries a commit time, so a downstream job can ask for only what changed since its last run instead of rescanning whole tables. Less compute, faster pipelines.

**Where it went:** Uber later donated Hudi to Apache. Like Iceberg at Netflix, Hudi is a table format born to fix a gap in the storage layer beneath it.

quiz.q: A downstream fraud job rescans Uber's full trips table every hour, but only a small share of trips changes each hour. Which Hudi feature fixes this, and how?
quiz.a: Incremental pulls. Hudi tags every change with a commit time, so the job asks only for records changed since its last run instead of rescanning the whole table.

mcq.q: What problem did Hudi solve for Uber?
options: Applying updates to immutable HDFS files quickly
Reducing NameNode memory used by small files
Moving HDFS data to Google Cloud Storage
Compressing trip data by reordering rows
mcq.why: Trip data changes after it's written; Hudi tracks commit times and file versions so updates land within minutes without rewriting partitions.

section: 7.3.2 Uber: from HDFS with Hudi to Google Cloud Storage
hook: Uber is moving one of the world's largest Hadoop deployments to Google Cloud. Its jobs won't change. How?
title: Uber is moving an exabyte-plus Hadoop lake to Google Cloud
body:
On May 30, 2024, Uber published its plan to move batch analytics and ML training from on-premises Hadoop to Google Cloud Platform. It called its installation one of the largest Hadoop deployments in the world, with tens of thousands of servers in each of its two regions.

The first phase swaps the storage for Google Cloud Storage. A connector implementing the Hadoop FileSystem interface lets existing jobs run without changes.

stat.label: of Uber Hadoop data moving to Google Cloud

takeaway: The best migration is one the jobs never notice.
deeper:
**The connector trick:** Jobs keep calling the same HDFS API. The connector translates those calls to Google Cloud Storage. The bytes live in a completely different system, and the code never knows.

**The phases:**
1. First phase: Google Cloud Storage becomes the lake storage, and the rest of the stack moves to cloud VMs as infrastructure as a service (IaaS).
2. Later phases: adopt managed services like Dataproc and BigQuery, which change more about how jobs run.

**Why Uber moved:** Its lake choices trace to mutable trip data first, which led to Hudi, and then to exiting data-center capital expense.

**The arc:** An HDFS lake that hit NameNode limits in 2016 to 2018, Hudi in 2017, and an object store announced in 2024. Both lake generations in one company.

quiz.q: Uber's first phase runs the stack on cloud VMs instead of jumping straight to BigQuery and Dataproc. Why?
quiz.a: Managed services would force changes to how jobs run. Keeping jobs on VMs behind the Hadoop FileSystem API changes only storage first, so existing jobs keep working untouched.

mcq.q: How do Uber's existing Hadoop jobs run unchanged on Google Cloud Storage?
options: A connector implements the Hadoop FileSystem interface
Jobs are rewritten automatically for BigQuery
GCS runs its own HDFS-compatible NameNode
Data is copied back to HDFS before each job
mcq.why: The cloud storage connector translates HDFS API calls to GCS, so jobs keep the same interface while the bytes move.

section: 7.3.2 Uber: from HDFS with Hudi to Google Cloud Storage
hook: You're about to migrate an exabyte-scale lake. One question decides how risky it will be. What is it?
title: Keep the narrowest interface stable while the bytes move
body:
Uber's cloud migration swapped the storage layer first, behind the same HDFS API, and left the jobs alone. That is the classic low-risk pattern: keep the interface, change the implementation, then modernize the layers above later.

When you plan a lake migration, ask: what is the narrowest interface I can keep stable while I move the bytes? That interface becomes your safety boundary.
takeaway: Change one layer at a time, so every failure has one suspect.
deeper:
**The diagnostic payoff:** Change storage and rewrite jobs at once, and when something breaks you can't tell which change did it. Change one layer and any failure points to that layer. Jobs also don't all need touching or retesting at the same time.

**Why narrow:** Here the interface is the Hadoop FileSystem API. Everything above it, the jobs, stays the same. Everything below it, the bytes, moves. The narrower the interface, the smaller the surface that must behave identically in the old and new worlds.

**Why layers make it possible:** A lake split into storage, file format and table format is exactly what allows one layer to be swapped under the others.

**The catch:** Modernizing the upper layers, such as adopting BigQuery or Dataproc, is still work. It just becomes a later, separate project once the bytes are safely in place.

quiz.q: Your team wants to move a lake to a new object store and rewrite its jobs for a new engine in the same quarter. What's the risk, and what order would you propose?
quiz.a: If something breaks, you can't tell whether storage or a rewritten job caused it. Move storage first behind the existing file-system API, verify, then rewrite jobs as a separate project.

mcq.q: Why is swapping storage behind an unchanged API a low-risk first step?
options: Failures can only come from the one layer that changed
It removes the need to copy any data
It makes every job run faster immediately
It avoids paying for cloud storage during tests
mcq.why: With jobs untouched, any breakage points to the storage layer, and jobs don't all need retesting at once.

hook: Meta ran tens of HDFS clusters per datacenter. Placing a dataset meant meeting two limits at once. Which?
title: Meta's HDFS warehouse became a 2D bin-packing puzzle
body:
Before Tectonic, Meta's data warehouse ran on HDFS. HDFS clusters had size limits, so Meta needed tens of clusters per datacenter and had to split datasets across them.

The Tectonic paper, presented at FAST 2021, calls this a two-dimensional **bin-packing** problem. Each dataset had to fit a cluster's capacity and its throughput at the same time. A dataset might fit the free space but overload the disks, or the reverse.
takeaway: Many small pools strand capacity. One big pool lets it flow.
deeper:
**What bin packing means:** Placing items into containers without exceeding their limits. With one limit it is hard enough. With two, space and IO throughput, leftover room in one dimension is often stranded because nothing fits the other.

**Where it came from:** The size limit of each HDFS cluster. A large warehouse had to be split, splitting created the puzzle, and running many independent systems added overhead of its own.

**Build, not buy:** Meta did not move to a public cloud. It built its own exabyte-scale file system, Tectonic, large enough to host the warehouse as one tenant among others. With 10× fewer clusters, far less splitting of datasets.

**The file layer:** Meta's reasons were exabyte scale and consolidating clusters, with ORC-based warehouse formats on top.

quiz.q: One of Meta's HDFS clusters had lots of free disk space, yet a new dataset couldn't go there. Why might that be?
quiz.a: Placement had two dimensions. The cluster may have had spare capacity but no spare throughput, so the dataset's IO would overload its disks. That space was stranded.

mcq.q: Which two limits made Meta's HDFS dataset placement a bin-packing problem?
options: Storage capacity and throughput
CPU cores and network ports
File count and replication factor
Latency and encryption overhead
mcq.why: Each dataset had to fit both the free space and the IO throughput of an HDFS cluster, which the Tectonic paper calls two-dimensional.

hook: One Meta storage cluster holds 10.7 billion files. What happened to the dozens of HDFS clusters before it?
title: Tectonic: 10× fewer clusters, 10.7 billion files in one
body:
**Tectonic** replaced three Meta systems: HDFS, Haystack and f4. Moving the warehouse onto it cut the number of warehouse clusters by 10 times. One multitenant production cluster in the paper had 1,590 PB of capacity, 1,250 PB used, 10.7 billion files and 4,208 storage nodes.

Redundancy follows lifetime. Long-lived warehouse data typically uses RS(9,6). Short-lived map-reduce shuffle output uses RS(3,3).
takeaway: Match redundancy to how long the data will live.
deeper:
**Escaping the ceiling:** 10.7 billion files in one cluster would be unthinkable for a single in-memory HDFS NameNode. Consolidating means fewer systems to run and far fewer datasets split across clusters.

**RS(9,6), long-lived:** 9 data chunks plus 6 parity chunks, about 1.67× raw space, surviving the loss of any 6. Strong protection at modest overhead suits data kept for years.

**RS(3,3), short-lived:** 3 data plus 3 parity, 2× space. More overhead, but only 6 chunks per stripe, so writes and reads are simpler. That suits shuffle output deleted soon after it is written.

**One system, many tiers:** Haystack and f4 were Meta's hot and warm blob stores. Folding them into Tectonic put hot blobs, warm blobs and the warehouse in one file system, with encoding chosen by how long data lives.

quiz.q: RS(3,3) uses 2× space while RS(9,6) uses about 1.67×. Why would Meta pick the more wasteful code for shuffle output?
quiz.a: Shuffle output is deleted soon, so long-term space cost barely matters. RS(3,3)'s shorter 6-chunk stripes make writing and reading simpler, which suits short-lived data.

mcq.q: What does RS(9,6) mean in Meta's Tectonic paper?
options: 9 data chunks plus 6 parity chunks
9 full replicas spread across 6 racks
6 data chunks plus 9 parity chunks
9 copies kept in 6 datacenters
mcq.why: Tectonic's RS(9,6) stores 9 data and 6 parity chunks, about 1.67× raw space, for long-lived warehouse data.

predict.q: Meta moved its data warehouse from HDFS onto Tectonic. By how much did the number of warehouse clusters drop?
options: 10 times
2 times
100 times

hook: Meta's warehouse hit a traffic spike and found spare disk IO it didn't own. Where did it come from?
title: Tectonic let the warehouse borrow the blob store's idle IO
body:
Give every workload its own cluster and each must be built for its own peak. Between peaks, the extra capacity sits idle.

Tectonic showed the alternative: **multitenancy**, where very different workloads share one storage system. Meta's warehouse and its blob storage were tenants of it. During traffic spikes, the warehouse could use spare disk IO from the blob-storage tenant. In separate clusters, that IO would have been stranded.
takeaway: Pooled resources absorb each tenant's peaks. Isolated ones waste them.
deeper:
**Different rhythms:** Warehouse jobs are bursty, with heavy scans at certain times. Blob storage has its own peaks. Dedicated clusters must each be provisioned for their own peak, and the gap between peak and average is waste.

**Pooling smooths it:** When the warehouse spikes, it draws on IO the blob tenant isn't using at that moment. Same logic as consolidating many HDFS clusters into fewer Tectonic ones: bigger pools strand less capacity, whether that capacity is disk space or disk throughput.

**Back to bin packing:** On small, isolated HDFS clusters, leftover throughput in one could never help another. In one large shared cluster, throughput becomes a shared resource.

**A cousin at Google:** Colossus has a similar goal, trying to keep its disks both full and busy while it places data by temperature.

quiz.q: Two workloads each peak at 100 units of disk IO, but never at the same time. Why might one shared cluster need less IO capacity than two dedicated ones?
quiz.a: Dedicated clusters must each be built for their own 100-unit peak. A shared cluster serves whichever tenant is peaking from IO the other isn't using, so its total can be lower.

mcq.q: How did multitenancy help Meta's warehouse during traffic spikes?
options: It used spare disk IO from the blob-storage tenant
It moved hot tables onto flash automatically
It throttled uploads to free network bandwidth
It cached warehouse files in blob-store memory
mcq.why: Sharing Tectonic with blob storage let the warehouse draw on the blob tenant's idle disk IO instead of that IO sitting stranded.

hook: BigQuery reorders your rows before storing them. You never asked it to. Why?
title: BigQuery's Capacitor reorders rows to compress better
body:
Shuffle a table's rows and its compressed size changes. The reason is **run-length encoding**, which stores a repeated value once plus a count, so it works best when identical values sit next to each other.

BigQuery stores tables in **Capacitor**, Google's internal columnar format, described in 2016. Finding the best row order for compression is NP-complete, so Capacitor uses a heuristic based on data types and query patterns to make run-length encoding work better.
takeaway: Compression depends on order. Put similar rows together and runs get longer.
deeper:
**Why it's hard:** Rows are shared across all columns. An order that makes long runs in one column can break runs in another. Finding the optimal order is NP-complete, with no known efficient exact algorithm, so Capacitor settles for a good heuristic.

**What sits underneath:** BigQuery is fully managed, and users never see files. Capacitor sits on Colossus, Google's cluster file system, which provides encryption at rest, Reed-Solomon coding and geo-replication.

**Maintenance you never schedule:** BigQuery re-optimizes storage in the background. In an open lake, that kind of work falls on platforms like LinkedIn's OpenHouse.

**The whole stack is Google's:** The format, the file system and the engine all belong to one company, and storage stays fully hidden from users.

quiz.q: A column holds country codes in random order across a billion rows. Why would sorting rows by country shrink it, and why can't Capacitor just sort perfectly for every column?
quiz.a: Sorted, identical codes sit together, so run-length encoding stores long runs cheaply. But one row order serves all columns, and the best overall order is NP-complete, so it uses a heuristic.

mcq.q: Why does Capacitor use a heuristic to choose row order?
options: Finding the optimal order is NP-complete
Run-length encoding ignores row order
Colossus stores rows only in arrival order
Users pick the row order for each table
mcq.why: The best row order for compression is NP-complete, so Capacitor uses data types and query patterns to pick a good one.

hook: Google's file system tries to keep its big disks both full and busy. Why is that harder than it sounds?
title: Colossus moves data from flash to big disks as it ages
body:
Big disks are cheap per byte but serve limited IOPS. Fill them with only cold data and they sit idle. Fill them with hot data and they can't keep up.

Colossus handles this by placing data by temperature. Google wrote in 2021 that hot data goes on flash and data moves to larger-capacity disks as it ages, while Colossus tries to keep disks both full and busy. This is tiering inside the file system, invisible to users.
takeaway: An empty disk and an overloaded disk both waste money.
deeper:
**Transparent tiering:** Neither applications nor BigQuery users pick a storage class. The system decides where bytes live. This is one of two ways to tier; the other sells tiers to customers as priced storage classes.

**Why the operator decides better:** Inside its own fleet, the operator can see real access rates, so it can move data by access and IOPS per TB instead of guesses. A customer choosing a class often has only an age like 30 days to go on.

**No retrieval fees:** Internal tiering happens in the provider's own fleet, so retrieval fees simply don't apply.

**A sibling:** Meta's f4 is another example of internal tiering, moving warm photos from Haystack's 3.6× effective replication to f4's 2.8×, then 2.1×. In both cases the user never sees the move.

quiz.q: Why can a system that tiers inside its own fleet do better than a customer choosing a cloud storage class?
quiz.a: The operator sees each byte's real access rate and moves data by IOPS per TB. A customer usually guesses from age or defaults, and pays retrieval fees when wrong.

mcq.q: Where does Colossus put data as it ages, according to Google in 2021?
options: From flash onto larger-capacity disks
From disk onto tape libraries
From one region to a cheaper region
From Capacitor files into row files
mcq.why: Google wrote that hot data goes on flash and moves to larger-capacity disks as it ages, invisible to users.

hook: Netflix, Uber, LinkedIn, Meta and Google all run giant lakes. No two chose the same stack. Why?
title: Five giant lakes, five stacks: change the layer that hurts
body: Each company changed the layer that hurt most. Netflix, a cloud-first company: S3, with Iceberg (created there) and Parquet. Uber: HDFS with Hudi for mutable trip data, now moving to GCS to exit data-center capex. LinkedIn: a large owned HDFS fleet, with Iceberg governance via OpenHouse. Meta: its own Tectonic, replacing HDFS, with ORC-based formats. Google: Colossus and Capacitor, hidden inside fully managed BigQuery.
takeaway: There is no right lake, only the right layer to change.
deeper:
**Table layer first:** Netflix is cloud-first, so S3 was natural, and its semantic gaps led Netflix to invent Iceberg. LinkedIn owns a large fleet and chose to modernize the table layer with OpenHouse instead of migrating storage.

**Storage layer next:** Uber first fixed its table layer, building Hudi because its trip data changes after it's written. Later, the capital expense of owning data centers pushed it toward GCS. Meta operates at exabyte scale and built Tectonic to collapse many HDFS clusters into far fewer.

**Whole stack:** Google integrates vertically: its own columnar format on its own file system, all hidden behind BigQuery.

**The pattern:** The layered model explains every row. Each company kept what worked and replaced the layer causing the pain.

quiz.q: LinkedIn and Uber both started with big HDFS lakes. One modernized its table layer, the other its storage. Which is which, and why?
quiz.a: LinkedIn kept its large owned HDFS fleet and added Iceberg governance through OpenHouse. Uber added Hudi for mutable trip data, then began moving storage to GCS to exit data-center capex.

mcq.q: Which company's lake storage is fully hidden from its users?
options: Google, with BigQuery on Colossus
Netflix, with Iceberg on S3
LinkedIn, with OpenHouse on HDFS
Uber, with Hudi on HDFS
mcq.why: BigQuery is fully managed; users never see files, while Capacitor and Colossus sit underneath.

hook: Meta traced two weeks of requests for photos, videos and attachments. How fast does interest die?
title: Day-old content gets over 100× the requests of year-old
body:
The best public evidence that data cools is Meta's f4 paper (OSDI 2014). It studied nine types of user **BLOBs** (Binary Large OBjects, like photos, videos and attachments) using a two-week trace.

For all nine types, content under a day old got more than 100 times the request rate of year-old content. For eight types, the rate fell 10 times in under a week. For six, it fell 100 times within 60 days.

stat.label: more requests: day-old vs year-old content

takeaway: Most data is cold, and it gets cold fast.
deeper:
**The size of the gap:** A 100-fold difference means storing new and year-old objects the same way either overspends on the old or starves the new.

**The speed of the drop:** A 10-fold fall within a week for eight of nine types means most demand arrives soon after upload. People view a new photo when it's posted, then rarely again.

**The lifecycle of a photo:**
1. Uploaded and hot, with many reads in the first day.
2. Reads drop about 10 times within a week.
3. Warm after about 1 to 3 months.
4. Cold: rarely read, kept for years.
5. Archived or deleted by retention policy.

**Why it matters:** This is the core fact of storage economics. A small hot part needs fast media; a large cold part needs cheap media.

quiz.q: A team keeps every photo, new or years old, on the same fast flash tier 'for simplicity'. Using the f4 findings, what's wrong?
quiz.a: Demand differs by over 100× between day-old and year-old content, and drops 10× within a week for most types. Flash money is wasted on photos almost nobody reads.

mcq.q: In Meta's f4 trace, how fast did request rates fall 10× for eight of nine BLOB types?
options: In less than a week
In about 60 days
In about three months
In about one year
mcq.why: For eight of nine types, requests dropped 10× in under a week; 60 days was the 100× drop for six types.

predict.q: Meta compared request rates for day-old and year-old user photos and videos. How big was the gap?
options: More than 100×
About 10×
About 3×

hook: Meta moved most kinds of user files to cheaper storage after a month. One kind never moved. Why?
title: Hot-to-warm: one month, three for photos, never for avatars
body:
Meta's f4 paper set safe cutoffs for moving BLOBs from hot to warm storage, one per type. For most types, one month was safe. Photos used three months. **Profile photos** were never moved: they stayed popular for about a year, keeping too many requests per TB for warm storage.

And warm objects dominate. More than 80% of objects in the oldest interval studied, and more than 89% in the newest, were warm for all types.
takeaway: Set cutoffs per data type. One global number fits nothing well.
deeper:
**Why one month was safe:** For most types, near-worst-case load fell below warm-tier capacity, about 20 IOPS per TB, within a week. Delete rates also fall with age. Waiting a month gave a comfortable margin on both counts.

**Why types differ:** Content cools at different speeds. A profile photo keeps getting requests for about a year after upload, so it never becomes cheap enough to serve from dense disks.

**Why warm matters most:** If more than 80% of objects are warm, the redundancy overhead of warm storage, not hot storage, drives total cost. That is the case for f4, which cut effective replication from Haystack's 3.6× to 2.8× and then 2.1×.

**The lesson:** A single global cutoff would either overload warm disks with profile photos or keep everything else hot too long.

quiz.q: You're told to apply a one-month hot-to-warm rule to every BLOB type at your company, because Meta did. What evidence would you ask for first?
quiz.a: Per-type near-worst-case load by age. Meta's month worked because most types fell below warm capacity within a week, but profile photos stayed popular about a year and never moved.

mcq.q: Why did Meta never move profile photos to warm storage?
options: They stayed popular for about a year
They were too small to erasure-code
Users deleted them within a month
They were kept only in the archive tier
mcq.why: Profile photos kept too many requests per TB for about a year, so warm disks couldn't serve them.

predict.q: Meta set a hot-to-warm cutoff for each BLOB type. When did profile photos move to warm storage?
options: Never
After one month
After three months

hook: Dense disks are cheaper per byte. So why can't you move data onto them as soon as it cools a little?
title: f4's warm tier could serve about 20 IOPS per TB
body:
A disk delivers a roughly fixed number of IOPS (input/output operations per second), however much it holds. In f4, 4 TB disks gave about 80 IOPS at acceptable latency. Divide 80 by 4: each stored terabyte gets about 20 IOPS.

So warm storage was sized for about 20 IOPS per TB. Data could move to dense storage only once its request rate per TB fell below that. Otherwise the disks couldn't keep up.

stat.label: IOPS per TB that f4's warm tier was sized for

takeaway: Dense disks are cheap because they hide many bytes behind few IOPS.
deeper:
**Tiering becomes arithmetic:** As disks get denser, IOPS per stored terabyte falls. The question for any dataset is simple: how many requests per second does each terabyte get? Above about 20 for f4, it would overload the disks and latency would suffer. Below, it can move and save money.

**Why hot data spreads:** Hot data needs flash or well-spread HDD. Spreading it thinly across many disks gives each terabyte more IOPS, at the cost of wasted capacity.

**Why cold data packs tight:** Cooling data asks for few IOPS, so it can fill disks densely.

**The same idea elsewhere:** Colossus tries to keep disks both full and busy. Full is about capacity; busy is about IOPS. Tiering is the art of hitting both.

quiz.q: A dataset peaks at 60 IOPS per TB. Can it move to an f4-style warm tier built from 4 TB disks serving 80 IOPS each?
quiz.a: No. Those disks give about 20 IOPS per TB, so 60 would overload them and hurt latency. Wait until its near-worst-case rate falls below about 20.

mcq.q: How did f4 arrive at about 20 IOPS per TB for its warm tier?
options: 4 TB disks each served about 80 IOPS
Each file was read about 20 times a day
Erasure coding added 20 extra reads per TB
The network allowed 20 requests per disk
mcq.why: Dividing about 80 IOPS per disk by 4 TB per disk gives roughly 20 IOPS for each stored terabyte.

hook: A cloud console suggests moving data to a cheaper tier after 30 days. Why is that number a trap?
title: Temperature is IOPS per TB. Age is only a proxy.
body:
Tiering tools usually ask for an age: move after 30 days. But temperature is a property of **IOPS per TB**, not of age. Age only correlates with access, sometimes badly.

Meta measured when each BLOB type's near-worst-case load, the 99th percentile, dropped below warm-tier capacity, and set the cutoff per type. When you design tiering, measure access per type and per age bucket. Don't pick 30 days because a console suggested it.
takeaway: Tier by what the disks can serve, not by the calendar.
deeper:
**Why the 99th percentile:** Averages hide bursts. A type might average well under warm capacity yet regularly spike above it, and when it does, latency suffers for everyone sharing those disks. Sizing to near-worst-case load keeps the warm tier safe.

**Why per type:** Types cool at different speeds. Profile photos never cooled enough, photos needed three months, most types needed one. One global cutoff would move profile photos too early and keep the rest hot too long.

**Why defaults are dangerous:** Round numbers like 30 days are starting points, not facts about your workload.

**The review question:** Ask for the access histogram: bytes read in the last 7, 30, 90 and 365 days, grouped by object age. Without it, tiering is guessing.

quiz.q: Two data types both average 10 IOPS per TB at 30 days old. One often bursts to 50; the other never exceeds 12. Warm disks serve about 20 per TB. Which can move?
quiz.a: Only the steady one. Cutoffs should follow 99th-percentile load, and the bursting type would overload warm disks during spikes even though its average fits.

mcq.q: Why did Meta set tiering cutoffs from 99th-percentile load instead of averages?
options: Averages hide bursts that would overload warm disks
The 99th percentile is cheaper to measure
Averages overstate how often data is read
Cloud consoles report only percentile data
mcq.why: A type can average under warm capacity but spike above it; sizing to near-worst-case load keeps latency safe for everyone on those disks.

hook: Storage is sorted into four temperatures. The dividing lines aren't about age. What are they about?
title: Hot, warm, cold, archive: four tiers, two questions
body: This morning's photo and one from 2012 should not sit on the same disks. **Storage tiering** matches media to how often data is read. Hot: read often, needs millisecond latency and high IOPS, on flash or well-spread HDD. Warm: read sometimes, still needs fast first byte, on dense HDD, often erasure-coded more aggressively. Cold: read rarely, on very dense HDD, sometimes powered down. Archive: read almost never, retrieval in hours is fine, on tape, powered-off disks or optical media.
takeaway: Each colder tier trades first-byte speed for cheaper bytes.
deeper:
**Each step down:** Media gets denser, with fewer IOPS per TB. Redundancy gets leaner, with more aggressive erasure coding, as in Meta's move from Haystack's 3.6× effective replication to f4's 2.8× and then 2.1×. Power drops, sometimes to zero when drives are powered down or tapes sit on shelves. Access latency rises from milliseconds to minutes or hours.

**The key phrase:** First byte, meaning the delay before data starts arriving. Warm storage still needs it fast, so readers don't notice. Cold and archive tiers relax that.

**Two questions pick the tier:** How often is the data read, measured as IOPS per TB? And how long can a reader wait for the first byte when it is read? Answer both and the tier mostly picks itself.

quiz.q: Old invoices are read a few times a year, but when an auditor asks for one, it's needed within seconds. Which tier fits, and why not archive?
quiz.a: Warm. Reads are rare, but the first byte must be fast, which warm still provides. Cold disks may be powered down, and archive retrieval takes hours.

mcq.q: What separates warm storage from archive storage?
options: Warm still needs fast first byte; archive accepts hours
Warm uses tape; archive uses dense HDD
Warm is never erasure-coded; archive always is
Warm data is always older than archive data
mcq.why: Warm data is read sometimes and needs quick first byte; archive data is read almost never, so hours of retrieval are fine.

hook: Inside Colossus, nobody picks a storage tier. On AWS, you pick one and pay for mistakes. Why the difference?
title: Tiering is either hidden in the system or sold as classes
body:
There are two ways to tier. **Transparent** tiering happens inside the storage system, which moves data between media or encodings itself. Colossus puts hot data on flash and cooling data on disk. Meta moved warm photos from Haystack (3.6× effective replication) to f4 (2.8×, then 2.1×).

Or tiering is **exposed** to the customer. Cloud providers sell tiers as storage classes with different prices, chosen by the customer or by an automated feature.
takeaway: Whoever sees the access data should make the tiering call.
deeper:
**Who decides:** In transparent tiering, the operator sees real access rates and moves data by IOPS per TB, as Meta did with f4. Users never choose, and there are no retrieval fees, because the provider owns the fleet.

**How the cloud signals cost:** In exposed tiering, prices do the talking: cheaper storage per GB, but retrieval fees, minimum durations and slower first byte. Customers must understand their own access patterns to choose well, or use features like S3 Intelligent-Tiering and GCS Autoclass.

**What transparent tiering saved:** Dropping warm photos from 3.6× to 2.1× effective replication means far less raw disk per byte. And since more than 80% of objects in f4's study were warm, that saving applied to most of the data.

quiz.q: Meta cut warm photos from 3.6× to 2.1× effective replication. Roughly what share of raw disk per warm byte did that save, and why did it matter so much?
quiz.a: About 40%, since 2.1 is roughly 58% of 3.6. It mattered because more than 80% of objects were warm, so the saving applied to most stored data.

mcq.q: What is a key difference between transparent tiering and cloud storage classes?
options: Transparent tiering needs no customer choice or retrieval fees
Transparent tiering always keeps data on flash
Storage classes move data by measured IOPS per TB
Storage classes are free to read but costly to store
mcq.why: Inside its own fleet the provider moves data itself; cloud classes make customers choose and pay retrieval fees and minimums.

hook: S3's coldest class stores data for about $1 per TB-month. Why doesn't everyone just put everything there?
title: Cooler tiers: cheap to store, pricey to read, minimum stay
body:
Every cooler tier makes the same deal: cheaper to store, more expensive to read, and a **minimum stay**. Delete early and you still pay for the remaining days.

S3 list prices in US East, checked in 2026, show the spread. Standard costs $0.023 per GB-month for the first 50 TB. Glacier Deep Archive costs $0.0018, about $1 per TB-month, but takes 12 to 48 hours to first byte and has a 180-day minimum.

stat.label: cheaper per GB: S3 Standard vs Deep Archive

takeaway: Cold tiers are cheap to keep and expensive to change your mind about.
deeper:
**The ladder, per GB-month:** Standard 0.023, falling to 0.021 at volume, no retrieval fee, no minimum. Standard-IA 0.0125, 30-day minimum. One Zone-IA 0.01, 30 days. Glacier Instant Retrieval 0.004, 90 days, still millisecond reads. Glacier Flexible Retrieval 0.0036, minutes to hours, 90 days. Deep Archive 0.0018, 12 to 48 hours, 180 days. Every class below Standard has a per-GB retrieval fee, though Flexible's bulk option is free.

**Flexible's three speeds:** Expedited in 1 to 5 minutes, standard in 3 to 5 hours, and free bulk in 5 to 12 hours.

**The catch:** Reading 1 GB back from a cool tier can cost as much as storing it for months. Tiering saves money only when data really is cold. Move data down and delete it soon after, and you pay the full minimum anyway.

quiz.q: You move logs to Glacier Deep Archive, then delete them after 60 days. What surprise is on the bill?
quiz.a: The 180-day minimum. Deleting at 60 days still charges the remaining 120 days, so the cheap tier costs far more than expected for data that short-lived.

mcq.q: Which trio describes every cooler storage tier's deal?
options: Cheaper storage, costlier reads, minimum stay
Cheaper storage, free reads, no minimum
Costlier storage, faster reads, minimum stay
Cheaper storage, faster reads, retrieval fees
mcq.why: Colder classes lower the per-GB storage price but add retrieval fees, minimum durations and usually slower first byte.

hook: S3 Standard-IA charges about half Standard's storage price. How often can you read an object before IA loses?
title: Read it more than once a month and Standard-IA loses
body:
Standard-IA saves about $0.0105 per GB-month over Standard (0.023 minus 0.0125). But its retrieval fee is about $0.01 per GB. Divide one by the other: the break-even is about one full read per month.

Read an object in full more often than that and IA costs more than Standard. For a photo archive, where most photos older than three months are read far less than monthly, IA wins easily. For an analytics table scanned daily, it loses.
takeaway: Break-even reads per month equal storage savings divided by retrieval fee.
deeper:
**The general rule:** For any tier, compare monthly storage savings per GB with expected monthly retrieval cost per GB. Break-even reads per month are roughly the savings divided by the retrieval fee. Plug in any tier's prices and the same division gives its break-even.

**A worked case:** An object read in full twice a month. IA saves about $0.0105 per GB-month, but two reads cost about 2 × $0.01 = $0.02 per GB. IA costs nearly twice what it saves. Keep it in Standard.
