**Same bucket, different answers:** One bucket can hold old photos that are rarely viewed and derived tables scanned every morning. That is why break-even math has to be done per data type.

**The minimum-stay trap:** IA's 30-day minimum means short-lived objects pay for a full month regardless.

quiz.q: A log file is read in full about once every three months. Is Standard-IA cheaper than Standard for it? Show the rough math.
quiz.a: Yes. IA saves about $0.0105 per GB-month, while reads average about $0.01 ÷ 3 ≈ $0.0033 per GB-month. Savings exceed retrieval cost, so IA wins.

mcq.q: Using the S3 prices given, why is roughly one full read a month the Standard-IA break-even?
options: IA saves about $0.0105/GB-month; a read costs about $0.01/GB
IA's 30-day minimum resets after every read
IA storage is exactly half of Standard's price
Each read moves the object back to Standard
mcq.why: Monthly storage savings of about $0.0105 per GB are wiped out by one full retrieval at about $0.01 per GB.

predict.q: S3 Standard-IA stores data for less than Standard but charges per GB read. Above what read rate does IA cost more?
options: About one full read a month
About ten full reads a month
About one full read a year

hook: One cloud's coldest tier makes you wait up to 15 hours. Another's answers in milliseconds. What's the catch?
title: Azure Archive is offline; GCS Archive reads in milliseconds
body:
Azure and Google offer the same tier shape as S3, with one big split at the bottom. Azure Blob Storage has hot, cool, cold and archive tiers, with 30-, 90- and 180-day minimums. Archive is offline: a blob must be **rehydrated**, copied back to an online tier, before it can be read, which can take up to 15 hours.

Google Cloud Storage has Standard, Nearline, Coldline and Archive. GCS Archive stays online, with millisecond first byte.
takeaway: An online archive saves you redesigning apps, and charges you for it.
deeper:
**The price of instant:** GCS Archive's convenience comes with higher retrieval fees and a 365-day minimum, twice the 180 days of Azure archive and S3 Deep Archive.

**Designing for offline:** With Azure archive, applications must request data, wait hours, and come back later. That is a different code path from reading any other blob. With up to 15 hours of rehydration, no user-facing read path can depend on it.

**The shared trap:** Azure charges early deletion pro-rata. Delete archived data before its minimum and you pay for the remaining days, just as on S3.

**How to choose:** If archived data is read only in disasters, an offline tier with slow retrieval is fine. If occasional reads must be immediate, an online archive avoids redesigning applications around delayed retrieval, at a price.

quiz.q: A legal team occasionally needs a years-old document within a minute of asking. Azure Archive or GCS Archive? What does the choice cost?
quiz.a: GCS Archive, which serves the first byte in milliseconds. You pay higher retrieval fees and a 365-day minimum. Azure Archive's up-to-15-hour rehydration would fail the one-minute need.

mcq.q: What must happen before a blob in Azure's archive tier can be read?
options: It must be rehydrated to an online tier
It must be restored from a tape backup
It must wait out the 180-day minimum
It must be copied to Google Cloud Storage
mcq.why: Azure archive is offline; a blob is rehydrated, copied back to an online tier, which can take up to 15 hours.

predict.q: Which of these coldest archive tiers still returns the first byte in milliseconds?
options: Google Cloud Storage Archive
Azure Blob Archive
S3 Glacier Deep Archive

hook: A few lines of JSON can manage your event logs from first write to final deletion. What do they say?
title: Lifecycle rules: after N days, move to class X or delete
body:
Nobody should hand-move logs between storage classes. A **lifecycle rule** is a bucket policy that does it: after N days, move objects matching a prefix or tag to class X; after M days, delete them. It runs automatically in the background.

A typical S3 rule for event logs keeps events in Standard for 30 days, then Standard-IA until 90 days, Glacier Instant Retrieval until a year, then Deep Archive. It deletes them after 2,555 days, about 7 years.
takeaway: The expiration line is a retention decision, often the biggest saving.
deeper:
**The shape follows cooling:** Events are hot for a month, warm until 90 days, instantly readable until a year, then deep archive. The rule mirrors how logs lose readers over time.

**Why Instant Retrieval next:** Between 90 and 365 days it keeps millisecond access for the odd investigation, at $0.004 per GB-month instead of Standard's $0.023. Deep Archive then holds the long tail at about $1 per TB-month.

**The line that matters most:** The expiration encodes a retention decision. At most companies, deleting data nobody needs saves more than any tier.

**The bigger role:** Lifecycle rules are how platforms enforce retention. A catalog of data types and their allowed ages becomes automatic transitions and deletes, scoped by prefix, like events/ here.

quiz.q: Your event-log rule moves data to IA, Glacier IR and Deep Archive, but has no expiration. Five years in, what keeps growing on the bill?
quiz.a: Every year of logs piles up in Deep Archive forever. Without an expiration, the rule only makes storage cheaper; it never removes the cost or the privacy risk.

mcq.q: What does the Expiration of 2,555 days do in the example event-log rule?
options: Deletes events after about 7 years
Moves events to Deep Archive after 7 years
Locks events against deletion for 7 years
Retries failed transitions for 7 years
mcq.why: Expiration deletes objects; 2,555 days is about 7 years, enforcing retention after the tier transitions.

hook: You set a rule to move billions of old log files to a cheaper class. The bill goes up. How?
title: Lifecycle traps: per-object fees, tiny objects, age ≠ access
body:
Lifecycle rules are simple but have three traps. Transitions cost money: each object moved is a billed request, so billions of small objects can make moving them expensive. Very small objects may cost more in a cool class, because of per-object overhead and minimum billable sizes, so batch them first.

And **age is not access**. Lifecycle rules move data by how old it is, not by whether anyone reads it.
takeaway: Tiering bills per object, so shrink the object count before you tier.
deeper:
**Two traps, one cause:** Transitions are billed per object, not per byte. A bucket of billions of tiny log files can cost more to move than the storage savings justify. Minimum billable sizes and per-object overhead inflate the effective price of each tiny object in a cool class.

**The fix:** Combine small objects into larger ones before tiering, the same remedy as for the small-files problem.

**The conceptual trap:** A lifecycle rule assumes old means cold. But an old dataset scanned by a monthly report gets moved to IA and racks up retrieval fees. Meanwhile a new object nobody reads sits in expensive Standard for 30 days.

**What came next:** The age-versus-access gap led providers to build access-based tiering, such as S3 Intelligent-Tiering and GCS Autoclass.

quiz.q: An old reference table is scanned in full by a report every week. A 30-day lifecycle rule moves it to Standard-IA. What happens to cost, and why?
quiz.a: Cost rises. Weekly full reads beat IA's roughly once-a-month break-even, so retrieval fees outweigh storage savings. The rule moved it by age, not access.

mcq.q: Why can lifecycle transitions be costly for billions of small log files?
options: Each object moved is a separately billed request
Transitions are billed per GB, not per object
Small files must be recompressed before moving
Cool classes reject objects under 1 MB
mcq.why: Transitions charge per object, and cool classes add per-object overhead and minimum billable sizes, so costs track object count, not bytes.

hook: Lifecycle rules move data by age, even data read every week. What does S3 offer when you can't predict reads?
title: S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves each object by its own reads
body:
**S3 Intelligent-Tiering** fixes the age-is-not-access problem by watching each object. After 30 days without access, an object moves to an Infrequent Access tier. After 90, to Archive Instant Access. Read it and it moves back to Frequent Access automatically.

There is no retrieval fee. Instead you pay a monitoring fee of $0.0025 per 1,000 objects per month.
takeaway: When you can't predict reads, pay per object to stop guessing.
deeper:
**The deeper options:** Archive Access (after at least 90 days) and Deep Archive Access (after at least 180 days) tiers can be turned on for data that tolerates retrieval delays.

**Why no retrieval fee matters:** With lifecycle rules, a dataset read more than expected can rack up retrieval fees. Here, a read just moves the object back to Frequent Access. The risk of a surprise bill goes away.

**The small-object exception:** Objects smaller than 128 KB are not monitored and always stay in Frequent Access. They never get cheaper, so batching small files is the only way to get them tiered here.

**Per-object pricing:** Because the monitoring fee is charged per object, fewer, larger objects keep it small. The service rewards the same file layout that compaction produces.

quiz.q: A bucket holds millions of 64 KB thumbnails nobody has viewed in a year. Will Intelligent-Tiering save money on them? Why?
quiz.a: No. Objects under 128 KB are not monitored and always stay in Frequent Access. Batch them into larger objects first so they can tier down.

mcq.q: What happens when an object in Intelligent-Tiering's Infrequent Access tier is read?
options: It moves back to Frequent Access with no retrieval fee
It is charged a per-GB retrieval fee
It stays put and its 30-day clock restarts
It is copied to Standard and billed twice
mcq.why: Intelligent-Tiering charges a monitoring fee instead of retrieval fees, and any read moves the object back to Frequent Access.

predict.q: S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves each object based on its reads. What happens to an object smaller than 128 KB?
options: It is never monitored or moved
It goes straight to the Archive tier
It pays a double monitoring fee

hook: Google's Autoclass charges no retrieval fees and no early-deletion fees. So what does it charge for?
title: GCS Autoclass: tiering by reads, a fee instead of penalties
body:
**GCS Autoclass** does for Google what Intelligent-Tiering does for S3. Objects move to Nearline after 30 days without access, Coldline after 90, and Archive after 365 if Archive is enabled as the terminal class. Reading an object's data moves it back to Standard. Objects under 128 KiB stay in Standard.

Autoclass charges a management fee, but no retrieval or early-deletion fees. Azure has lifecycle policies and, more recently, a smart tier.
takeaway: Know your access pattern? Use rules. Don't? Pay for tiering by access.
deeper:
**Azure's version:** The smart tier moves data between hot, cool and cold automatically. Combined with lifecycle management policies, Azure offers both age-based and access-based tiering.

**Four approaches, side by side:** Lifecycle rules move by age, prefix and tag, charge retrieval fees, and suit predictable data like logs and backups. Intelligent-Tiering moves each object by access, with a monitoring fee instead of retrieval fees. Autoclass does the same with a management fee. Both suit unknown or mixed access. Internal tiering in Colossus or f4 moves by access and IOPS per TB, with no retrieval fees at all.

**The shared blind spot:** Intelligent-Tiering and Autoclass both leave objects under about 128 KB in the top tier. Tiny objects gain nothing from either.

quiz.q: Nightly backups are written, kept 90 days, then deleted, and are almost never read. Autoclass or lifecycle rules? Why?
quiz.a: Lifecycle rules. The pattern is predictable, so age tracks access well, and you avoid a per-object management fee. Access-based tiering pays off when reads are unknown or mixed.

mcq.q: What happens when an Autoclass object sitting in Coldline is read?
options: It moves back to Standard
It is charged a retrieval fee
It is charged an early-deletion fee
It moves down to Archive
mcq.why: Autoclass returns read objects to Standard and charges a management fee instead of retrieval or early-deletion fees.

hook: A tiering plan lands in your design review. One chart decides whether it's engineering or guessing. Which?
title: Demand the access histogram before any tiering plan
body:
In a design review, ask for the **access histogram**: for each data type, how many bytes were read in the last 7, 30, 90 and 365 days, grouped by object age.

Without it, tiering is guessing. With it, you can compute each tier's break-even: whether retrieval fees, minimum durations and monitoring fees are outweighed by the storage savings for that data type. The histogram turns a debate about opinions into arithmetic.
takeaway: No histogram, no tiering plan. Measure first, then move bytes.
deeper:
**Why by age:** Grouping reads by object age shows how fast each type cools, just as Meta's f4 study did for nine BLOB types.

**Why by type:** One global rule mistreats data that behaves differently, like profile photos versus attachments.

**What each window tells you:** The 7-day window shows what is truly hot. The 30- and 90-day windows line up with common minimum durations and the thresholds Intelligent-Tiering and Autoclass use. The 365-day window shows whether anything is read after a year, which decides between deep archive and deletion.

**What it unlocks:** Apply the Standard-IA test: bytes read in full more than about once a month lose money in IA. And spot types whose bytes are never read at all, which raises a better question: why keep them?

quiz.q: The histogram shows one data type had zero bytes read in the last 365 days, at every age. What's the most valuable next question?
quiz.a: Why are we keeping it at all? Before tiering it to Deep Archive, check its retention requirements: deleting it saves more than any tier.

mcq.q: What does an access histogram for tiering group reads by?
options: Data type and object age
Bucket name and region
Object size and file format
User and time of day
mcq.why: Bytes read in the last 7, 30, 90 and 365 days, per data type and grouped by age, show when each type crosses tier break-evens.

hook: Some data must be kept for decades and will probably never be read. What should its storage optimize?
title: Archival: keep it for decades, read it almost never
body:
Backups, legal holds, raw sensor data, old media masters, financial records: data you must keep but expect almost never to read. That is **archival**.

The goals change completely. Lowest cost per TB-year. Very high durability. Long media life. Latency in hours is acceptable. That last point opens the design space: tape, powered-down disks and even experimental glass become options, trading access speed for cost and longevity.
takeaway: Hours of patience buy the cheapest, longest-lived bytes.
deeper:
**Archive versus cold:** Cold data might be read occasionally. Archive data is kept mostly as insurance or to meet an obligation.

**Why TB-year:** Horizons are long, so the right unit is total cost over years, not a monthly price.

**Why durability and media life:** Data may sit untouched for decades, and nobody notices corruption unless something checks. A medium that fails or becomes unreadable in five years forces repeated copying, the hidden cost of every archive.

**What hours buy:** Robots can fetch tapes. Drives can stay off until needed. Reads can be batched. Whole datacenters can be built without backup power, as Meta did for cold storage. The options run from cloud archives near $1 per TB-month to Microsoft's research on glass.

quiz.q: Two archive options cost the same per GB-month. One's media lasts 5 years, the other's decades. Over a 30-year retention, why might the second be far cheaper?
quiz.a: The 5-year media must be copied to new media several times, each an expensive, risky migration. Cost per TB-year over the whole horizon, not monthly price, is the right comparison.

mcq.q: Which set of goals defines archival storage?
options: Lowest cost per TB-year, high durability, long media life
Lowest latency, high IOPS, frequent access
Highest throughput, columnar layout, local reads
Fast first byte, no minimum, no retrieval fee
mcq.why: Archive data is kept for years and rarely read, so cost over time, durability and media life matter; hours of latency are fine.

hook: Is Amazon Glacier stored on tape? Some blog posts claim to know. What does Amazon actually say?
title: Nobody publishes what media the cloud archive tiers use
body: AWS, Google and Microsoft do not publish what media their archive tiers use. Be careful with blog posts that claim to know. What you can compare is the **service contract**. S3 Glacier Deep Archive: 12 to 48 hours to first byte, about $1 per TB-month, 180-day minimum, launched 2019. Glacier Flexible Retrieval: minutes to 12 hours, $0.0036 per GB-month, the original Glacier from 2012. GCS Archive: milliseconds, 365-day minimum. Azure Archive: up to 15 hours to rehydrate, 180-day minimum.
takeaway: Reason from the service contract, not from rumors about the hardware.
deeper:
**What the shape hints:** Retrieval delays of hours leave room for robotic media like tape libraries, powered-down drives, or batching many reads before touching the media. That is an inference, not a fact.

**Why it matters:** Assuming Glacier is tape is tempting, but it is not publicly confirmed. Claims you can't source weaken everything else you say. Talk about what the contract guarantees instead.

**The GCS contrast:** GCS Archive is online, with millisecond first byte, paid for with higher retrieval fees and a 365-day minimum. The hours-long delays of Azure Archive and Deep Archive give those providers room for slower, cheaper arrangements.

**How to choose:** Match the contract (first-byte latency, minimum duration, storage price, retrieval fees) to how urgently you'll read your archive and how long you'll keep it.

quiz.q: A colleague argues Glacier Deep Archive must be tape because retrieval takes 12 to 48 hours. How would you correct the reasoning?
quiz.a: Providers don't publish their archive media. Hours of delay only leave room for tape, powered-down drives or batched reads; they don't prove any one of them.

mcq.q: What do AWS, Google and Microsoft publish about their archive tiers' media?
options: Nothing: they don't publish the media
That all archive tiers use LTO tape
That archive tiers use powered-down HDDs
That archive tiers use optical discs
mcq.why: The providers publish service terms, not media; hours-long retrieval only suggests room for tape, powered-down drives or batched reads.

hook: Ransomware can encrypt every online copy of your data. What's one copy it physically can't touch?
title: Tape: cheap, powerless on a shelf, and air-gapped
body:
Ransomware or a buggy script with write access can reach every online copy. Magnetic tape, today mostly **LTO** (Linear Tape-Open), is the oldest archive media still in wide use, and it has three strengths. Very low cost per TB of media. No power while a cartridge sits on a shelf. And an **air gap**: a cartridge in a library slot cannot be deleted by ransomware or a software bug.

The weakness is access: a robot loads the cartridge and the drive winds to the spot, taking tens of seconds to minutes.
takeaway: Software can only destroy what it can reach.
deeper:
**The unique strength:** Online systems, however well replicated, are reachable by software. A malicious actor or buggy code with write access can delete or encrypt every online copy. A cartridge in a slot is disconnected from all of that until it's loaded.

**Still growing:** The LTO Program reported 152.9 EB of new LTO capacity shipped in 2023 and 176.5 EB in 2024. These are compressed-capacity figures, so raw capacity is lower. LTO-10 was introduced in 2025. Inside hyperscalers, though, public evidence of tape use is limited.

**The main risk:** Drive generations become obsolete. An LTO drive reads only a few generations back, so old cartridges must eventually be copied forward to newer media.

**The irony:** Tape can last decades if stored well. The drives that read it don't.

quiz.q: An attacker gains admin access to all your online storage, including every replica. Which copy survives, and why?
quiz.a: A tape cartridge sitting in a library slot. It is disconnected, so no software can delete or encrypt it until it is loaded into a drive.

mcq.q: What is tape's main weakness as archive media?
options: Access takes tens of seconds to minutes
It needs constant power while on the shelf
Ransomware can erase idle cartridges
It costs more per TB than flash
mcq.why: A robot must load the cartridge and the drive must wind to the right spot, which takes tens of seconds to minutes.

predict.q: Is the amount of new tape capacity shipped each year growing or shrinking?
options: Growing
Roughly flat
Shrinking

hook: Three replicas protect you from a dead disk. What protects you from your own code deleting the data?
title: Gmail 2011: a bug deleted mail, and tape brought it back
body:
In February 2011, a software bug deleted Gmail data for a small share of users. Google restored it from tape backups, and its blog said it backs Gmail up to tape to protect against exactly such bugs. It is the best-known public case of tape inside a hyperscaler.

Replicas protect against hardware loss. But a software bug replicates instantly to every copy. Only an offline, separate copy protects against that.
takeaway: Replication copies your mistakes as faithfully as your data.
deeper:
**Replication is not backup:** Replication keeps synchronized copies so a failed disk, server or datacenter loses nothing. But synchronization works both ways. If software deletes or corrupts data, every replica gets the same change. All copies are then equally wrong.

**The offline copy:** Tapes are written separately and sit disconnected, so a bug in the live system cannot reach them. Restoring from tape is slow, but it is possible.

**The design-review question:** When someone says data is safe because it has three replicas, ask what happens if the application deletes it. Replicas and erasure coding answer the hardware question. Only separate, offline copies answer the software question.

**A cousin:** Immutability features like S3 Object Lock block deletion until a set date, protecting against both mistakes and ransomware.

quiz.q: Your service keeps 3 replicas in 3 regions. A deploy ships a bug that deletes user records. Which copies still have the data, and what would?
quiz.a: Likely none of the replicas, since the deletions replicate to every copy. A separate offline copy, such as a tape backup, or a copy locked against deletion would survive.

mcq.q: Why can't replication alone protect data from a deletion bug like Gmail's in 2011?
options: A software bug's changes reach every replica
Replicas are always kept in one datacenter
Replication only runs once a day
Replicas lack checksums to detect loss
mcq.why: Replicas guard against hardware loss, but a bug's deletions propagate to all copies; only a separate offline copy like tape is safe.

predict.q: In 2011 a software bug deleted Gmail data for some users. What did Google restore it from?
options: Tape backups
Replicas in another datacenter
Copies in users' mail clients

hook: Meta built datacenters with no backup generators and most drives switched off. Why wasn't that reckless?
title: Meta cold storage: an exabyte per hall, under 1/6 the power
body:
Meta, then Facebook, built dedicated cold storage datacenters in Prineville, Oregon and Forest City, North Carolina, described in 2015. Each data hall could hold up to one exabyte. UPS systems and generators were removed, because cold data can wait for power to return. Only one drive per tray was powered on at a time.

Durability came from software: **erasure coding** across drives and racks kept data safe while hardware was off.

stat.label: of the power of Meta's normal datacenters

takeaway: If the data can wait, the building doesn't need to stay on.
deeper:
**The rack:** A rack held 2 PB on 4 TB drives and used about one-quarter the power of normal storage servers. With most drives off, power draw falls sharply.

**The code:** Reed-Solomon stored each 1 GB as 10 data plus 4 parity chunks, 1.4 GB in total, so data survives the loss of any 4 chunks.

**The scanner:** Every drive was checked about every 30 days for silent corruption, damage nobody would otherwise notice because the data is rarely read.

**Why no generators was safe:** Availability was not the goal. If power fails, cold data is briefly unreachable, but nobody urgently needs it, and erasure coding keeps it durable while hardware is offline. The main risk of powered-down disks is a drive failing to spin up.

quiz.q: A power outage takes one of Meta's generator-free cold storage halls down for a day. What is lost, and what isn't?
quiz.a: A day of availability, which cold data can tolerate. No data is lost: it is erasure-coded 10+4 across drives and racks, so it survives hardware being offline.

mcq.q: How did Meta's cold storage encode 1 GB of data?
options: 10 data plus 4 parity chunks, 1.4 GB total
3 full replicas, 3 GB total
6 data plus 3 parity chunks, 1.5 GB total
9 data plus 6 parity chunks, about 1.67 GB total
mcq.why: Reed-Solomon with 10 data and 4 parity chunks stored 1 GB as 1.4 GB and survives losing any 4 chunks.

hook: Normal datacenters are built never to go down. Meta built one that was allowed to. What did that buy?
title: Design the whole datacenter for one data temperature
body:
Normal datacenters are built for constant availability: redundant power, every drive spinning, low latency. Cold data needs none of that.

Meta's cold storage accepted that cold data can wait, and designed the whole datacenter around it. It removed power redundancy, powered most drives off and cut power per rack. Software made those compromises safe: erasure coding protected against unavailable drives, and reads were scheduled to the one powered drive in each tray.
takeaway: Relax one requirement fully, and savings appear everywhere else.
deeper:
**Scheduling reads:** Only one drive per tray is powered at a time, so the software has to send each read to the drive that is on. Hardware and software were designed together around that constraint.

**Surviving the off switch:** Erasure coding with 10 data and 4 parity chunks means data survives drives that are off, failed or unreachable. A scanner checks every drive about every 30 days for silent corruption.

**Tiering, scaled up:** Tiering moves data to cheaper media. Meta built cheaper buildings. The longer and colder the data, the more access speed you can trade for cost, as long as durability is handled in software.

**Neither half works alone:** Powered-off drives without erasure coding would be a durability risk. Erasure coding without the relaxed building would save far less power.

quiz.q: You're designing a facility for old security footage that is rarely viewed. Which of Meta's cold-storage choices would you borrow, and what software must come with them?
quiz.a: Drop UPS and generators, and power most drives off. Pair that with erasure coding across drives and racks, reads scheduled to powered drives, and periodic scans for silent corruption.

mcq.q: What made Meta's powered-off drives safe for durability?
options: Erasure coding across drives and racks
Three full replicas on spinning disks
Battery backup on every drive tray
Nightly copies of all data to tape
mcq.why: Reed-Solomon 10+4 coding let data survive drives that were powered off, failed or unreachable.

hook: Meta showed off a Blu-ray disc rack for cold storage in 2014. Why treat its savings claims with suspicion?
title: Meta's Blu-ray rack: a prototype, not a proven product
body:
Meta showed a Blu-ray optical disc cold storage rack as a prototype at the Open Compute Summit in 2014, pitched as cheaper and lower-power than disk-based cold storage. Capacity and savings numbers circulated in the press, but no primary Meta source with verified figures could be found.

Meta also published no long-term production results. Its later FAST 2021 paper describes Tectonic as the system that replaced Haystack and f4 for blob storage. Treat optical as an experiment.
takeaway: A demo shows possibility. Production data shows viability.
deeper:
**The media profile:** Optical, in the Blu-ray prototype, has access times of seconds to minutes, uses no power at rest, and claims media life of decades. Its main risks are low density and limited adoption.

**The evidence rule:** Storage media claims often spread through press coverage and blog posts with numbers nobody can trace to a primary source. The same caution applies to claims about which media cloud archive tiers use.

**How to evaluate archive tech:** Prefer published production results and papers over demos and announcements. Treat unsourced figures as unverified, however often they are repeated.

**Why archives care most:** You will trust this media with data for decades. A prototype with no long-term production record tells you little about year twenty.

quiz.q: A vendor pitches a new archive medium with impressive capacity numbers from a trade-show demo. What evidence should you ask for before trusting it?
quiz.a: Primary sources: published papers or long-term production results. Demo and press numbers are unverified; Meta's Blu-ray prototype never published production results.

mcq.q: Why should Meta's Blu-ray cold storage rack be treated as an experiment?
options: Meta published no long-term production results
Blu-ray discs need constant power to keep data
It was shown to lose data within five years
Tectonic was built on top of optical media
mcq.why: It was a 2014 prototype with no verified figures from a primary Meta source and no published long-term production results.

hook: Magnetic media needs copying to new media every 5 to 10 years. Could any medium skip that for millennia?
title: Project Silica: data in glass for thousands of years
body:
Magnetic media must be copied to new media every 5 to 10 years. **Project Silica**, Microsoft Research's work on quartz glass, aims to end that. A femtosecond laser writes tiny 3D changes called **voxels** in layers inside a glass platter. A microscope reads them with polarized light, and machine learning decodes the image back to bits.

The glass is expected to last thousands of years or more. It is research, not a product.

stat.label: raw capacity of one DVD-sized glass platter

takeaway: The best migration plan is media that never needs one.
deeper:
**What Microsoft has published:** A platter about the size of a DVD holds raw capacity above 7 TB. A proof of concept with Warner Bros. was announced in 2019.

**The library design:** A 2023 SOSP paper described a full library with separate read, write and storage racks and robotic shuttles. It met a 15-hour service level objective for archive reads, even with read drives of only 30 MB/s.

**Write-once, both ways:** Once written, glass cannot be overwritten. That protects stored data against accidental or malicious changes, a bit like tape's air gap, but it also means the medium can never be reused.

**Where archives are going:** Media that needs no power, no refresh and no migration. Silica is not there as a product yet, but it shows the direction.

quiz.q: An archive team keeps data for 30 years and re-copies it to new media every few years. What would Silica change, and what can't it do that their media can?
quiz.a: It would remove migrations, since glass is expected to last thousands of years without power or refresh. But it can't be overwritten, and it's still research, not a product.

mcq.q: How does Project Silica read data back from glass?
options: A microscope with polarized light, decoded by machine learning
A femtosecond laser that rewrites each layer as it reads
A magnetic head scanning across the platter surface
A standard Blu-ray drive reading the platter's surface
mcq.why: Voxels written by a femtosecond laser are imaged with polarized light, and machine learning decodes the images back into bits.

hook: Four archive media all use almost no power at rest. So what actually separates them?
title: Disk, tape, optical, glass: pick the risk you can live with
body: Four archive media, and all use almost no power at rest. What separates them is life and risk. **Powered-down HDD** (Meta's cold storage): seconds to minutes to access, about 5 years of life, main risk a drive failing to spin up. **Tape (LTO)**: tens of seconds to minutes, decades if stored well, risk that drive generations become obsolete. **Optical** (Blu-ray prototype): seconds to minutes, claimed decades, low density and limited adoption. Glass (Silica research): hours in the library design, thousands of years claimed, not yet a product.
takeaway: Media life is useless without a working reader.
deeper:
**Access time first:** Always slow compared with online storage, which is fine for archives.

**Power at rest:** Nearly zero at rest for all four. That is the core cost advantage over spinning disks.

**Lifetime and risk:** Powered-down disks are the most familiar technology but have the shortest life, and an idle drive may not spin up when finally needed. Tape lasts decades physically, but drives read only a few generations back. Optical claims long life but never reached wide adoption or high density. Glass claims the longest life by far but is research.

**The column to read first:** Main risk. It names what will actually cause data loss or expense decades from now. The common thread is that you need both surviving media and working readers, which is why migration dominates long-term archive cost.

quiz.q: Your archive must survive 50 years, and it must use media you can buy today. Which option from the four fits best, and what's its weak point?
quiz.a: Tape: decades of media life if stored well, and in wide use. Its weak point is readers, since drives read only a few generations back, so you'll still need migrations.

mcq.q: What is the main risk of powered-down HDD archives?
options: A drive failing to spin up
Readers becoming obsolete after decades
Low density and limited adoption
Not yet being a product
mcq.why: Powered-down disks last about 5 years, and a drive left idle may fail to spin up when it's finally needed.

section: 7.6.6 Migration is the hidden archive cost
hook: Your archive's price per TB-month looks tiny. What cost isn't on the price tag yet?
title: Migration: the archive cost that isn't on the price tag
body:
Archive readers become obsolete. An LTO drive reads only a few generations back, and HDDs last about five years. So an archive must be re-copied to new media several times over a 30-year retention.

At exabyte scale, each migration is a major project: read everything back, write it to new media, verify it. The cloud provider doing this for you is a big reason cloud archive is attractive. Removing it is the main promise of glass.
takeaway: An archive's real price includes every future copy.
deeper:
**Why it's hidden:** The cost doesn't show up when you first store data. The day-one price per TB-month leaves out the future labor, hardware and risk of copying everything forward every five to ten years.

**The count:** 30 years on media lasting 5 to 10 years means three to six media generations, so two to five full migrations.

**The risk:** Every copy is a chance to lose or corrupt data. Migrations also compete for the limited read throughput archives are built around.

**Build versus buy:** A company running its own tape archive must plan and staff these migrations. A cloud archive customer pays a monthly price and the provider absorbs them. When you compare options, put migration in the total cost of ownership.

quiz.q: You compare a self-run tape archive and a cloud archive for 30-year retention using only day-one cost per TB. What did you leave out, and who pays it in each case?
quiz.a: Two to five media migrations as drives become obsolete. With self-run tape you plan, staff and fund them; with a cloud archive the provider absorbs them in its monthly price.

mcq.q: How many full migrations does 30-year retention need on media lasting 5 to 10 years?
options: Two to five
Three to six
One or two
Six to ten
mcq.why: 30 years spans three to six media generations; moving between them takes one fewer migration, so two to five.

predict.q: You must keep an archive for 30 years on media that lasts 5 to 10 years. How many full migrations will it need?
options: Two to five
None, if stored well
Ten or more

hook: Some rules force you to keep data. Others force you to delete it. How does one policy obey both?
title: Retention: minimum from law, maximum from privacy and cost
body:
Tiering decides where data lives. **Retention** decides how long. A retention policy sets, per data type, the minimum time it must be kept and the maximum after which it must be deleted.

Minimums come from law and business: financial records, audit logs, legal holds. Maximums come from privacy law and cost. GDPR's storage-limitation principle means personal data should not be kept longer than needed, and every extra day costs money and raises breach risk.
takeaway: Every data type needs two dates: keep-until and delete-by.
deeper:
**How platforms enforce it:**
1. Data is created with a type tag.
2. A retention catalog maps each type to minimum and maximum days.
3. The platform applies lifecycle rules and TTLs (time to live) from the catalog.
4. If a legal hold is active, data is kept and deletion is blocked.
5. Otherwise data tiers down, is deleted at its maximum age, and the deletion is recorded in an audit log.

**An illustration, not legal advice:** Raw click events deleted after 2 years (cost, privacy). Audit logs kept 7 years (compliance). Photos kept until the user deletes them (user contract).

**Enforcing the minimum:** S3 Object Lock and Azure immutable blob storage block deletion until a date, protecting against both mistakes and ransomware. The maximum is enforced by the deletes themselves, and the audit log proves they happened.

quiz.q: Click events have a 2-year maximum, but legal puts them under a hold at month 23. What should the platform do at month 24?
quiz.a: Keep them. An active legal hold blocks deletion, overriding the maximum. Once the hold lifts, the data is deleted and the deletion recorded in an audit log.

mcq.q: Where does maximum retention come from?
options: Privacy law and cost
Audit and financial record rules
Legal holds from courts
Minimum storage durations
mcq.why: GDPR's storage-limitation principle and the cost and breach risk of keeping unneeded data set the maximum; law and business set the minimum.

hook: An admin with full write access runs a script that deletes your audit logs. What can stop it?
title: Object Lock turns a retention minimum into a guarantee
body:
A retention minimum written in a policy doc depends on everyone following it. A mistaken script, a careless admin or ransomware can still delete the data early.

Immutability features close that gap. **S3 Object Lock** and **Azure immutable blob storage** block deletion until a set date. They protect against both mistakes and ransomware, so the minimum becomes a technical guarantee rather than a promise.
takeaway: A policy asks people to behave. A lock doesn't have to ask.
deeper:
**How it fits retention:** When the catalog says audit logs must be kept 7 years, a lock ensures no one, even with write access, deletes them before the date. Legal holds work similarly: while a hold is active, deletion is blocked.

**Why ransomware loses:** Ransomware typically encrypts or deletes data and demands payment. If data can't be deleted until a date, the attack can't destroy those copies. It's the same idea as tape's air gap and the Gmail lesson: software can reach every online copy unless something blocks it.

**The flip side:** Locked data can't be removed to honor the maximum side of retention, or a user's deletion request, until the lock expires. So lock periods must be set deliberately per data type, alongside the catalog, lifecycle rules and audit logs.

quiz.q: A team locks all user profile data with Object Lock for 10 years, 'to be safe'. A user asks for their data to be deleted. What's the problem?
quiz.a: The lock blocks deletion until it expires, so the team can't honor the request or the privacy maximum. Lock periods must match each type's retention, not a blanket safety margin.

mcq.q: What do S3 Object Lock and Azure immutable blob storage do?
options: Block deletion until a set date
Encrypt data so ransomware can't read it
Move data to an offline archive tier
Delete data automatically at its maximum age
mcq.why: They enforce the retention minimum by preventing deletion until a date, protecting against both mistakes and ransomware.

hook: Your rule deletes raw click events after 2 years. Years later, those clicks still live in your lake. Where?
title: Deleting raw data while its copies live on
body:
A common mistake is setting a deletion rule on the raw data but not on its copies. A deleted event still lives in derived tables, ML training sets, backups and caches.

Retention has to follow the **lineage**: the chain of datasets built from the original. Otherwise the policy is enforced on paper while the data survives everywhere else. LinkedIn's OpenHouse builds retention into the table platform itself for this reason.
takeaway: Retention that ignores lineage deletes the original and keeps the evidence.
deeper:
**How far one event travels:** A click can flow into a daily active users table, an ad report and an ML training set, with backups and caches along the way. Deleting it from the raw log does little if those copies persist.

**The cost side:** Derived tables may be as large as the raw data they came from.

**The compliance side:** GDPR's storage-limitation principle applies to personal data wherever it lives, so a forgotten copy can still break the maximum retention rule.

**Why a platform:** Following lineage means knowing what was derived from what and applying policy across all of it. That is hard team by team. LinkedIn put retention, data purging and partition expiration into OpenHouse next to compaction and snapshot expiration, so every table it manages gets the policy automatically.

quiz.q: An audit finds a deleted user's personal data in last year's ML training set, though the raw events were purged on time. What went wrong, and what's the structural fix?
quiz.a: Retention covered raw data only, not its lineage. Build retention into the table platform so derived datasets, training sets and backups inherit the deletion policy.

mcq.q: What must a retention policy follow to actually delete data?
options: The data's lineage into every derived copy
The storage class the raw data sits in
The age of the oldest partition only
The bucket's lifecycle transition schedule
mcq.why: Deleted raw data survives in derived tables, training sets, backups and caches, so retention must cover every dataset built from it.

hook: Your team plans a clever tiering system to cut the storage bill. What question should come first?
title: The cheapest byte is the byte you deleted
body:
Before you build a clever tiering system, ask: why are we keeping this at all? At most companies, a retention review saves more than any tiering project.

Tiering lowers the price per byte. Moving from S3 Standard to Deep Archive cuts it about 12 to 13 times. Deletion cuts it to zero. It also removes breach risk, future migration costs and privacy exposure, none of which tiering touches.
takeaway: Tiering shrinks the price per byte. Retention shrinks the byte count.
deeper:
**The stark comparison:** A dataset in Deep Archive still costs about $1 per TB-month, month after month. Someone still has to migrate it to new media over the decades, and that cost is baked into the price. And it still counts as stored personal data for privacy purposes. A deleted dataset costs nothing.

**Why teams tier instead:** Tiering is a technical challenge, so engineering effort flows there. Retention is a policy question that needs legal, product and data owners in the room. Harder organizationally, but often a bigger win.

**How they work together:** The retention catalog sets how long each type lives. Lifecycle rules tier data down during that window and delete it at the end.

**The first question:** In any review of a growing storage bill, start with which data does not need to exist.

quiz.q: Moving a dataset from S3 Standard to Deep Archive cuts its storage price about 12×. Name three costs that move leaves in place but deletion would remove.
quiz.a: Ongoing storage at about $1 per TB-month, future media migrations, and the privacy and breach exposure of keeping the data at all.

mcq.q: Why does a retention review often save more than a tiering project?
options: Deletion removes bytes; tiering only lowers their price
Retention reviews are cheaper to automate
Tiering adds retrieval fees to every object
Deep Archive costs more than S3 Standard
mcq.why: Tiering cuts cost per byte about 12 to 13× at best; deleting unneeded data cuts it to zero and removes risk too.

hook: Lakes, tiers, archives, retention. If you keep one rule from each, which should it be?
title: Lakes to archives: the rules worth keeping
body: A lake separates storage from compute and wants cheap, high-throughput bytes. HDFS hit NameNode memory and 3× replication limits. Object stores fixed those but lost locality and atomic rename, which table formats replaced. Small files are permanent, so compaction is a platform service. Data cools fast, and temperature means IOPS per TB. Cooler tiers need break-even math. Archive media wins on cost but hides migration. Retention beats tiering.
takeaway: Most bytes are cold: measure them, tier them, and delete what you can.
deeper:
**Two paths off HDFS:** Uber announced in 2024 a move of its more-than-1-exabyte Hadoop lake to Google Cloud, starting by swapping HDFS for GCS behind the same API. Meta instead replaced HDFS with its own Tectonic and cut warehouse clusters by 10 times.

**The evidence:** Meta's f4 data showed request rates falling 10 times within a week for most BLOB types, and more than 80% of objects warm in older intervals.

**Tiering mechanics:** Move data to dense media when its access rate falls below what that media can serve. Cooler tiers trade lower storage price for retrieval fees, minimum durations and slower first byte. S3 Intelligent-Tiering and GCS Autoclass fix age-is-not-access but ignore objects under 128 KB.

**Archives and retention:** Tape, powered-down disk and glass research win on cost and power, but migration is a hidden cost. Set minimum and maximum retention and apply them across all copies.

quiz.q: A company's storage bill doubles every year. In what order would you apply retention, compaction and tiering, and why?
quiz.a: Retention first: delete what needn't exist. Then compaction, to cut per-file and per-request costs. Then tiering guided by an access histogram, so each type moves only when break-even math says so.

mcq.q: Which limitation do S3 Intelligent-Tiering and GCS Autoclass share?
options: Objects under about 128 KB are never moved
They charge a retrieval fee on every read
They move data by age instead of access
They cannot move data to archive classes
mcq.why: Both leave objects smaller than about 128 KB in the frequent or standard tier, so tiny files gain nothing.
